sbh1.3:1.1: What is the stage of renunciation?
sbh1.3:1.3: the going to dispassion by the worldly path,
sbh1.3:1.4: the going to dispassion by the supramundane path,
sbh1.3:1.5: and the requisites for these two — gathered into one, this is called the stage of renunciation.
sbh1.3:1.6: What is going to dispassion by the worldly path?
sbh1.3:1.7: When someone here sees grossness in the realm of desire,
sbh1.3:1.8: and sees calm in the seclusion-born joy and pleasure of the first dhyāna, both as attainment and as rebirth:
sbh1.3:1.9: so seeing, abiding much in that, he attains dispassion [Conjectural: from the realm of desire],
sbh1.3:1.11: So, above each dhyāna, he becomes a seer of grossness in all the lower planes
sbh1.3:1.12: and a seer of calm in all the upper planes; so seeing, abiding much in that, he attains dispassion all the way up to the sphere of nothingness,
sbh1.3:1.13: And he attains the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
sbh1.3:1.14: The going to dispassion by the worldly path goes no higher, no further than this.
sbh1.3:1.15: What is the going to dispassion by the supramundane path?
sbh1.3:1.16: When someone here, one who frequents good persons, learned in the noble dharmas, knows suffering as suffering as it actually is,
sbh1.3:1.21: thereafter, further cultivating the path, he disjoins and releases himself from the dharmas of the three realms — those to be abandoned by [the path of] vision and [the path of] cultivation — and thus passes beyond the three realms.
sbh1.3:1.22: This is called going to dispassion by the supramundane path.
sbh1.3:2.3: wholesome dharma-desire, restraint of virtue, [Lacuna] knowing the right measure in food, application to wakefulness in the early and late watches of the night, dwelling with full awareness, association with good friends, hearing-and-reflection on the true dharma, [practice] without obstacle, generosity, the ornament of the recluse — these dharmas are called the requisites for going to worldly and supramundane dispassion.
sbh1.3:2.4: Of these, endowment-from-self, endowment-from-others, and wholesome dharma-desire — their division is to be understood as before,
sbh1.3:2.5: namely as stated [above] regarding the lesser supporting condition for the perfecting of the seed.
sbh1.3:2.7: When someone here dwells endowed with virtue, [and so on] up to ‘having undertaken them, he trains in the precepts of training’.
sbh1.3:2.8: And how does he dwell endowed with virtue,
sbh1.3:2.9: [and so on] up to ‘having undertaken them, he trains in the precepts of training’?
sbh1.3:2.10: How does he dwell endowed with virtue?
sbh1.3:2.11: When, in the precepts undertaken, his bodily action is unimpaired and his [Conjectural: verbal] action unimpaired,
sbh1.3:2.12: his conduct unbroken, his conduct unrent — thus is he endowed with virtue.
sbh1.3:3.1: How is he restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa?
sbh1.3:3.2: The sevenfold leading-out virtue is called the restraint of the Prātimokṣa.
sbh1.3:3.3: These, by the division of assemblies, become many restraints.
sbh1.3:3.4: Here, however, taking the monastic (*bhikṣu*) restraint specifically, [the text] says ‘restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa.’
sbh1.3:3.5: How is he endowed with proper conduct?
sbh1.3:3.6: When, with respect to deportment, duties-to-be-performed, or application to the wholesome side, he is endowed with conduct that conforms to the world and does not transgress the world, conforms to the Vinaya and does not transgress the Vinaya.
sbh1.3:3.8: How does he avoid transgressing the world and avoid transgressing the Vinaya [in this respect]?
sbh1.3:3.9: He walks where one should walk,
sbh1.3:3.10: and walks as one should walk —
sbh1.3:3.11: [walking] in such a way that he is not blamed by the world, by the good, by the properly engaged, by good persons, by his co-religionists, by the Vinaya-holders, by those trained in Vinaya; he is not censurable,
sbh1.3:3.12: not in a position to be reproached.
sbh1.3:3.13: As with walking, so with standing, sitting, and lying down — [the same applies].
sbh1.3:3.15: How does he avoid transgressing the world,
sbh1.3:3.16: [how does he avoid] transgressing the Vinaya? — [These] are called the duties-to-be-performed:
sbh1.3:3.19: [the use of] water and the tooth-stick,
sbh1.3:3.21: taking and bringing back alms-food, eating,
sbh1.3:3.22: the cleaning and putting away of the bowl,
sbh1.3:3.24: the laying out of the lodging —
sbh1.3:3.25: and, in summary, bowl-work and robe-work.
sbh1.3:3.26: Whatever else is of this kind is called a duty-to-be-performed.
sbh1.3:3.27: These, as appropriate — wherever they are to be performed and however they are to be performed — he performs there and in that manner,
sbh1.3:3.28: such that he is not criticized by worldlings, not censured;
sbh1.3:3.29: by the Vinaya-holders and those trained in Vinaya, he is not blameworthy, not censured;
sbh1.3:3.30: by the properly engaged co-religionists [likewise]. Thus conduct grounded in duties-to-be-performed is conduct that does not transgress the world
sbh1.3:3.31: and does not transgress the Vinaya.
sbh1.3:4.1: [Third,] conduct grounded in application to the wholesome side.
sbh1.3:4.2: How is this non-transgressive of the world and non-transgressive of the Vinaya?
sbh1.3:4.3: The wholesome side is said to be:
sbh1.3:4.4: recitation, respectful acts toward and attendance on teachers, looking after the sick, mutually arousing compassionate mind, engagement in giving consent (*chandadāna*), inquiry and hearing of Dharma by one adroit and not lazy, performing bodily service for wise co-religionists, rousing others to the wholesome side, teaching Dharma,
sbh1.3:4.5: entering retreat, sitting cross-legged — these and other such dharmas are called
sbh1.3:4.7: He, accordingly — as has been proclaimed,
sbh1.3:4.8: wherever it is to be performed — performs it in just that way,
sbh1.3:4.9: such that he is not blameworthy,
sbh1.3:4.10: not censured by worldlings, by Vinaya-holders, by those trained in Vinaya, by the properly engaged, by good persons, or by his co-religionists. This is called conduct grounded in application to the wholesome side, [conduct] non-transgressive of world and Vinaya.
sbh1.3:4.11: Conduct complete in these modes is called completeness of conduct;
sbh1.3:4.12: Thus he is endowed with proper conduct.
sbh1.3:4.13: And how is he endowed with proper resort?
sbh1.3:4.14: Five are the non-resorts for a monk.
sbh1.3:4.16: A cowherd settlement, a prostitute’s house, a tavern, the royal household, and fifth, the households of caṇḍālas and *kaṭhina*s.
sbh1.3:4.17: He who avoids these non-resorts rejected by the Tathāgata, and who at the right time frequents elsewhere — the blameless resort — is endowed with proper resort.
sbh1.3:5.1: How does he see danger in the slightest fault?
sbh1.3:5.3: the minor and lesser precepts of training, in which transgression and rising-out are recognized —
sbh1.3:5.4: transgression of those is the slightest fault.
sbh1.3:5.5: Again, since rising-out from such transgression is accomplished with little difficulty, it is therefore called slightest.
sbh1.3:5.6: How, then, does he see danger [in it]?
sbh1.3:5.7: He reflects: ‘On account of this transgression I might become unfit for attaining what has not yet been attained, for realizing what has not yet been realized, for directly realizing what has not yet been directly realized; I might go to the lower realms, might become one bound for the lower realms; I would reproach myself, or the Teacher would reproach me, or the deities, or wise co-religionists would censure me in accordance with Dharma;
sbh1.3:5.8: and in all directions and intermediate directions an evil report, repute, word and verse about me would arise’ — he sees danger in these [Conjectural: disagreeable] dharmas, present and future, that have that [transgression] as their cause.
sbh1.3:5.9: By this he does not [Conjectural: deliberately] transgress even those minor and lesser precepts of training, even for the sake of life.
sbh1.3:5.10: If at some time, on some occasion, through forgetfulness he transgresses, he quickly, very quickly makes amends according to Dharma and rises out [of the transgression].
sbh1.3:5.11: Thus he sees danger in the slightest fault.
sbh1.3:5.12: How does he train by undertaking the precepts of training?
sbh1.3:5.14: Previously, when receiving the restraint of the Prātimokṣa by the formal act of a motion and three announcements at his full ordination, he heard the formulation of only a few precepts; the remaining precepts, over [Conjectural: two] hundred, set forth in the Prātimokṣa-sūtra, he took on by pledge alone, [saying] ‘I shall acquire them in all respects.’
sbh1.3:5.15: Having heard from his preceptor and instructor, from those he talks with, converses with, is acquainted with and is dear to, and from the half-monthly recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra,
sbh1.3:5.16: and thereby, from the undertaking of all the trainings, the restraint of the Prātimokṣa is obtained. Thereafter, the precepts of training in which he is skilled he does not transgress, and if he has transgressed he makes amends according to Dharma. But as for those precepts of training in which he is [Conjectural: not yet] skilled, his understanding not yet developed:
sbh1.3:5.17: those precepts previously undertaken by way of pledge he now undertakes through developed skill [in their actual content],
sbh1.3:5.18: [doing so] on the basis previously proclaimed, [namely] from the preceptor or instructor, as before.
sbh1.3:5.19: And having thus undertaken [them] through developed skill, he trains as instructed, neither lessening nor adding.
sbh1.3:5.20: In the precepts of training taught by those who stand in a teacher’s place, he grasps both meaning and letter undistortedly.
sbh1.3:5.21: Thus he trains by undertaking the precepts of training. — Such, in this much, is the detailed division of the restraint of virtue.
sbh1.3:6.1: What, then, is the summary meaning?
sbh1.3:6.2: This summary meaning has just three marks.
sbh1.3:6.3: [That is,] the aggregate of virtue is elucidated by the Blessed One under three marks: the mark of non-loss, the mark of own-nature, and the mark of own-nature-with-its-qualities.
sbh1.3:6.4: How so? — In that he says ‘he dwells endowed with virtue,’ by this the non-loss mark of the restraint of virtue is declared.
sbh1.3:7.1: In that he says ‘restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa,’
sbh1.3:7.2: by this the own-nature mark is declared.
sbh1.3:7.4: ‘endowed with proper conduct and proper resort,’
sbh1.3:7.5: by this — with reference to others — the quality-mark of the restraint of the Prātimokṣa as undertaken is declared.
sbh1.3:7.6: For when others observe his fullness of conduct and resort, those without confidence gain confidence, and those already confident become still more so;
sbh1.3:7.7: those with confidence perform acts grounded in confidence.
sbh1.3:7.8: And they do not defile their minds,
sbh1.3:7.9: they do not send forth blame. Otherwise, for one endowed with virtue, conduct and resort, this quality and benefit dependent on others would [not] be; and in the reverse case there would be fault.
sbh1.3:7.11: ‘seeing danger in the slightest faults, having undertaken them, he trains in the precepts of training,’
sbh1.3:7.12: by this the mark of the quality-and-benefit dependent on oneself is declared.
sbh1.3:7.13: For what reason? [Although] this person, endowed with proper conduct and resort, would gain the quality-and-benefit dependent on others,
sbh1.3:7.15: having ruined virtue, by that cause, by that condition he is reborn in the lower realms,
sbh1.3:7.16: or becomes unfit for the attainment of the not-yet-attained, [as] above.
sbh1.3:7.17: Now since he sees danger in the slightest fault —
sbh1.3:7.18: still more in the major [faults] — and trains by undertaking the precepts of training, by that cause, by that condition, at the breaking up of the body he is reborn in a happy destiny,
sbh1.3:7.19: or becomes fit for the attainment of the not-yet-attained, [as] above. For this reason [the foregoing] is called the quality-and-benefit of the restraint of virtue dependent on oneself.
sbh1.3:8.2: in brief, the Blessed One has elucidated [under three rubrics] undertaken-virtue, leading-out virtue, and the cultivation of virtue.
sbh1.3:8.4: ‘he dwells endowed with virtue,’ by this undertaken-virtue is declared.
sbh1.3:8.6: ‘restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa,’ by this leading-out virtue (*nairyāṇika*) is declared.
sbh1.3:8.7: For the virtue subsumed under the restraint of the Prātimokṣa is called the training in higher virtue (*adhiśīla*).
sbh1.3:8.8: And on the basis of the training in higher virtue, he cultivates the training in higher mind (*adhicitta*) and the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) — and thus, for the destruction of all suffering,
sbh1.3:8.10: That is, on the basis of higher virtue, taking it as forerunner — therefore the restraint of the Prātimokṣa is called leading-out virtue.
sbh1.3:8.12: ‘endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault, having undertaken them, he trains in the precepts of training’ — by this the cultivation of virtue is declared.
sbh1.3:8.13: By these modes that virtue of the restraint of the Prātimokṣa is to be cultivated,
sbh1.3:8.14: and so cultivated, it becomes well cultivated. Thus this single restraint of virtue is to be understood as set forth by a six-mode teaching.
sbh1.3:9.1: This restraint of virtue is to be understood as deficient by ten modes,
sbh1.3:9.2: and conversely, by ten causes, [as] perfected.
sbh1.3:9.3: By what ten causes is it deficient?
sbh1.3:9.4: It is ill-grasped from the very beginning; it is too slack; it is too overreaching; it is gripped by heedlessness and indolence;
sbh1.3:9.6: it is gripped by deficiency of conduct; it is gripped by deficiency of livelihood; it is fallen into the two extremes; it is not leading out; and it is fallen from the undertaking. Here, how is virtue ill-grasped from the very beginning?
sbh1.3:9.7: When someone here goes forth under pressure from a king, or under pressure from thieves, or distressed by debt, or distressed by fear, or in fear for his livelihood — not for the sake of recluseship, not for the sake of brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*), not for the calming of self, not for the restraint of self, not for the final nirvāṇa of self — thus from the very beginning
sbh1.3:9.10: When someone here is shameless, with weak remorse,
sbh1.3:9.11: loose, doing loosely what is taught in the training — this is excessive slackness.
sbh1.3:10.2: When someone here is an ill-grasper, feeling regret in the wrong place —
sbh1.3:10.3: feeling regret in cases where [Conjectural: no regret] is called for;
sbh1.3:10.4: in the wrong place he produces toward others a contemptuous mind or [Conjectural: a malicious] one,
sbh1.3:10.5: and admonishes them. Thus it is too overreaching.
sbh1.3:10.6: How is it gripped by heedlessness and indolence?
sbh1.3:10.7: When someone here, with respect to the past, has fallen into transgression,
sbh1.3:10.8: and some of it, through forgetfulness, he has not atoned for according to Dharma;
sbh1.3:10.9: as with the past, so with the future and the present — whatever transgression he has fallen into,
sbh1.3:10.10: and some of it, through forgetfulness, is not atoned for according to Dharma;
sbh1.3:10.11: and he does not, in advance, undertake intense effort for the sake of non-transgression in the future, [resolving]
sbh1.3:10.12: ‘Let me act in such a way that, acting and dwelling [so], I would not commit transgression’ — yet so he acts, so he dwells,
sbh1.3:10.14: Endowed with this heedlessness connected with the past limit, the future limit, and the middle limit — along with heedlessness about what should have been done earlier — he holds dear the pleasure of sleep, lying down, and resting on the side;
sbh1.3:10.15: he becomes unskilled, lazy, lacking energy [to rise up]; he does not perform bodily service for his wise co-religionists. Thus engaged, he is gripped by heedlessness and indolence.
sbh1.3:11.2: When someone here lives the holy life having resolved:
sbh1.3:11.3: ‘By this virtue, observance, austerity, holy life, I shall become a god or some [other] kind of divine being,’ desirous of gain and honor.
sbh1.3:11.4: He seeks gain and honor from others;
sbh1.3:11.5: he yearns for gain and honor.
sbh1.3:11.7: How is it gripped by deficiency of conduct?
sbh1.3:11.8: When someone here, having undertaken either deportment, or duties-to-be-performed, or application to the wholesome side, transgresses the world
sbh1.3:11.9: and transgresses the Vinaya, [as detailed] above — thus it is gripped by deficiency of conduct.
sbh1.3:11.10: How is it gripped by deficiency of livelihood?
sbh1.3:11.11: When someone here has great desires, is discontented, [Conjectural: hard to feed, and hard to support],
sbh1.3:11.13: not by Dharma — and seeks alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites by non-Dharma,
sbh1.3:11.15: and for the sake of robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites — for the sake of generating regard [for himself in others] — he displays to others a contrived, deliberately composed deportment: non-restless faculties, non-fickle faculties, calm faculties,
sbh1.3:11.16: by which others, having generated regard for his qualities, think [that things] should be given, [things] should be done —
sbh1.3:11.17: namely, robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites.
sbh1.3:11.19: brazen, affected, parading his name and clan; he is much-learned,
sbh1.3:11.20: a Dharma-holder, and from a gain-motive alone he speaks Dharma to others — what was spoken by the disciples — or his own qualities, real or somewhat exaggerated, he himself proclaims.
sbh1.3:11.21: Or he has others say it, or shows it by hints; or, wanting a robe or some other recluse’s requisite, much or finer, though not in want he displays a shabby robe,
sbh1.3:11.22: [thinking]: ‘Faithful brāhmaṇas and householders, noticing his want of a robe, will think that a plentiful and fine robe should be given.’
sbh1.3:11.23: As with the robe, so with any other recluse’s requisite — when he does not obtain it at will from faithful brāhmaṇas and householders, or when [their] possessions are lacking or absent — by importunity he begs,
sbh1.3:11.24: pressing them and speaking harshly. Or, having obtained an inferior thing when possessions are present, he derogates that gain, depreciates it,
sbh1.3:11.25: and in front of the giver-patron speaks thus:
sbh1.3:11.26: ‘Ho, son of good family, there are sons and daughters of good family who, compared with you, are lower in clan and poorer, and yet give thus and so, fine and pleasing gifts.
sbh1.3:11.27: Why do you, higher in clan than they and [Conjectural: richer], give what is not pleasing, not fine, and meager?’
sbh1.3:11.28: He who by such modes — relying on hypocrisy (*kuhanā*), on flattery (*lapanā*), on insinuation (*naimittikatā*), on extortion (*naiṣpeṣikatā*), on gain-seeking-by-gain (*lābhena lābhaṁ niścikīrṣā*) — seeks robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites from others,
sbh1.3:11.30: and what is by non-Dharma is for him wrong livelihood.
sbh1.3:11.31: Thus that virtue is gripped by deficiency of livelihood.
sbh1.3:11.32: How is it fallen into the two extremes?
sbh1.3:11.33: When someone here is bent on the pleasure of sense-desires, supremely attached to them.
sbh1.3:11.34: He uses the robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites — obtained either by Dharma or by non-Dharma —
sbh1.3:11.35: without seeing the danger, without knowing the escape. This is called one extreme.
sbh1.3:11.36: And again, here someone is bent on self-mortification; in manifold ways he scorches and torments himself.
sbh1.3:11.39: an ash-taker, one whose resort is the pestle,
sbh1.3:11.40: one whose resort is the plank,
sbh1.3:11.41: one who stays in a squat, applied to the yoga of exertion while squatting,
sbh1.3:11.43: up to three times [a day] he tends the fire; a water-immerser —
sbh1.3:11.44: up to three times [a day] he immerses in water;
sbh1.3:11.45: standing on one foot, he turns with the sun.
sbh1.3:11.46: Such, or any other such kind of application to self-mortification — this is called the second extreme.
sbh1.3:11.47: Thus it is fallen into the two extremes.
sbh1.3:11.48: How is it not leading out?
sbh1.3:11.49: When someone here clings to virtue or observance by [wrong] view:
sbh1.3:11.50: ‘By this very virtue or observance there will be purification,
sbh1.3:11.52: All the virtue of those outside — even well-guarded, even well-purified — with such purity is [still] called not leading out.
sbh1.3:11.53: Thus it is not leading out.
sbh1.3:11.54: How is it fallen from the undertaking?
sbh1.3:11.55: When someone here is wholly, entirely shameless, indifferent
sbh1.3:11.57: of evil virtue, of evil dharma, inwardly rotten, oozing, become as refuse,
sbh1.3:11.59: not a recluse but claiming to be a recluse, not a celibate but claiming to be celibate — thus it is fallen from the undertaking.
sbh1.3:11.60: By these ten causes virtue is deficient — this is called by the Blessed One the deficiency of virtue.
sbh1.3:11.61: Moreover, the Blessed One also spoke of [Conjectural: the calamity] of virtue.
sbh1.3:11.62: And that is to be understood from two of these causes:
sbh1.3:11.63: not-leading-out and falling from the undertaking; by the other causes only deficiency of virtue is to be understood.
sbh1.3:11.64: From these very causes set on the dark side, by their reverse — by the bright-side causes — the fullness of virtue is to be understood,
sbh1.3:11.66: In some places, again, the Blessed One speaks of virtue by the word ‘root.’
sbh1.3:11.67: As said: ‘He is one whose root is well-established, delighting in the calming of the mind,
sbh1.3:11.68: [beings are] bound and unbound through view, the evil and the noble’ — so the verse.
sbh1.3:12.1: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘ornament.’
sbh1.3:12.2: As stated: ‘A monk or nun endowed with the ornament of virtue abandons the unwholesome, cultivates the wholesome.’
sbh1.3:12.3: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘ointment.’
sbh1.3:12.5: ‘A monk or nun endowed with the ointment of virtue,’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:12.6: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘scent.’
sbh1.3:12.7: ‘There is, [Conjectural: Ānanda], that kind of scent whose scent wafts downwind, against the wind, and both with and against the wind.’
sbh1.3:12.8: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘good conduct’ (*sucarita*).
sbh1.3:12.10: ‘The fruit of good bodily conduct is to be desired in the visible-here-and-now and in the after-state; likewise of good verbal conduct.’
sbh1.3:12.11: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘restraint.’
sbh1.3:12.13: ‘The giver, the donor, becomes endowed with virtue,
sbh1.3:12.14: established in restraint, grounded in scriptural learning and view, seeing the fruit.’
sbh1.3:12.17: restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa,’ [as elaborated above] in detail.
sbh1.3:12.18: For what reason did the Blessed One speak of virtue by the word ‘root’?
sbh1.3:12.19: Because the meaning of ‘root’ is the meaning of establishment, the meaning of basis.
sbh1.3:12.20: This very virtue is the establishment, the basis, for the arising and attainment of all worldly and supramundane pure, blameless, supreme, distinguished, pleasant-fruited dharmas; therefore it is spoken of by the word ‘root.’
sbh1.3:12.21: Just as the earth is the establishment, the basis, for the arising of grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees, just so [is] virtue, [as detailed] above.
sbh1.3:12.22: For what reason is virtue declared by the word ‘ornament’?
sbh1.3:12.24: Those other adornments — necklaces, bracelets, armlets, rings, garlands of gold and silver — only as long as one is young,
sbh1.3:12.25: youthful, with dark hair, possessing the freshness of youth, do those adornments, when put on him, [actually] adorn.
sbh1.3:12.26: But not so for one aged, old, weak, octogenarian or nonagenarian, broken-toothed, gray-haired — on such a one those adornments, put on, appear on the contrary as if mocking [him].
sbh1.3:12.27: In sickness, in loss of wealth, in loss of kin — when these befall — he does not shine [in such adornments].
sbh1.3:12.28: Virtue, however, is an adornment for all [people], at all times.
sbh1.3:12.29: Therefore it is spoken of by the word ‘ornament.’
sbh1.3:13.1: For what reason is virtue spoken of by the word ‘ointment’?
sbh1.3:13.2: Here, the great wholesome, blameless undertaking of virtue removes the bodily and mental burning caused by every undertaking of bad conduct (*dauḥśīlya*) —
sbh1.3:13.3: as for one scorched by heat in the great-summer-burning time, sandal ointment or camphor ointment [removes the burning]. For this reason virtue is spoken of by the word ‘ointment.’
sbh1.3:14.1: For what reason is virtue called ‘scent’?
sbh1.3:14.2: For a virtuous individual, in all directions and intermediate directions, fair fame, repute, voice, [and] eulogy go forth —
sbh1.3:14.3: just as, of various kinds of root-scents, sap-scents, or flower-scents, when wafted in the directions, an agreeable scent goes forth.
sbh1.3:14.4: For this reason virtue is spoken of by the word ‘scent.’
sbh1.3:15.1: For what reason is virtue called ‘good conduct’?
sbh1.3:15.2: ‘This conduct leads to ease, this conduct leads to heaven, leads to good destinies.’
sbh1.3:15.3: Therefore it is called good conduct.
sbh1.3:16.1: For what reason is virtue called ‘restraint’?
sbh1.3:16.2: This dharma has cessation [of unwholesome dharmas] as its own-nature, has the mark of cessation, has abstention as its own-nature.
sbh1.3:16.3: Therefore it is called by the word ‘restraint.’
sbh1.3:16.4: Of this restraint of virtue, the threefold review is the cause of purification.
sbh1.3:16.6: Namely: review of bodily action, review of verbal action, review of mental action.
sbh1.3:16.7: Reviewing these [three kinds of] action, he purifies the restraint of virtue.
sbh1.3:16.8: Whatever action he intends to perform with the body, that he reviews [thus]:
sbh1.3:16.9: ‘Is this bodily action of mine harmful to myself or others, unwholesome, giving rise to suffering, with painful result? Or is this bodily action of mine non-harmful to myself and others, wholesome, giving rise to ease, with pleasant result?’ If, reviewing thus, he knows: ‘this bodily action of mine is harmful to myself or another, unwholesome, [Conjectural: giving rise to suffering, with painful result],’ then, having so reviewed, he does not engage in it;
sbh1.3:16.10: that action he does not do,
sbh1.3:16.12: If, again, he knows: ‘this bodily action of mine is non-harmful, wholesome,’ [the rest] as before, that he does —
sbh1.3:16.13: that bodily action he does not withhold, but performs.
sbh1.3:16.14: Even an action that, with reference to past time, has been done by him through the body —
sbh1.3:16.16: ‘Was this [action] of mine harmful?’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:16.17: If, reviewing thus, he knows: ‘this action of mine is harmful,’ [the rest] as before,
sbh1.3:16.18: in the presence of wise co-religionists he withholds,
sbh1.3:16.20: Even an action that, with reference to past time, has been done by him through the body —
sbh1.3:16.22: ‘Was this [action] of mine harmful?’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:16.23: If, reviewing thus, he knows: ‘this action of mine is harmful,’ [the rest] as before,
sbh1.3:16.24: in the presence of wise co-religionists he confesses, [and] makes amends according to Dharma.
sbh1.3:16.25: If, on the other hand, reviewing thus, he knows: ‘this bodily action of mine is non-harmful,’ [the rest] as before,
sbh1.3:16.26: by that very joy and gladness he dwells, day and night, much in training. Thus that bodily action of his is well reviewed
sbh1.3:16.28: namely, in past, future, and present times.
sbh1.3:16.29: As with bodily action, so verbal action is to be understood.
sbh1.3:16.30: Mind arises dependent on past formations;
sbh1.3:16.31: mind arises dependent on future and present formations.
sbh1.3:16.33: ‘Is this mind of mine harmful?’ [the rest] as before,
sbh1.3:16.34: up through: he does not produce [it];
sbh1.3:16.37: Conversely, on the bright side, he produces [it], does not withhold, [but] performs that mental action.
sbh1.3:16.38: Thus that mental action is by him reviewed
sbh1.3:16.40: namely, in past, future, and present times.
sbh1.3:16.41: For what reason? In past time, in future time, and in present time, whatever recluses or brahmins, having reviewed and purified bodily, verbal, and mental action, have lived extensively [in this way] — all of them have done so by such review and purification,
sbh1.3:16.42: as was said by the Blessed One concerning the Venerable Rāhula:
sbh1.3:16.43: ‘Bodily action, then verbal action, and also mental action, Rāhula —
sbh1.3:16.44: repeatedly review [them], remembering the instruction of the Buddhas.
sbh1.3:17.1: This is the work of the recluse — train in this, Rāhula.
sbh1.3:17.2: For one training therein, there is only good, not evil.’
sbh1.3:18.1: Here, that he investigates ‘bodily action, verbal action, mental action — is this harmful for me?’ [the rest] as before — this is the review.
sbh1.3:18.2: And that some [actions] he withholds and confesses, some he performs,
sbh1.3:18.3: and by that very joy and gladness — training day and night — he dwells much [in training] — this is called purification.
sbh1.3:18.4: Of the restraint of virtue thus purified, ten benefits are to be understood.
sbh1.3:18.6: [1] Here a virtuous individual dwells reviewing his own purity of virtue and gains non-regret; for one free of regret there is gladness; for one of gladdened mind joy arises;
sbh1.3:18.7: with a joyful mind the body becomes pliant;
sbh1.3:18.8: with pliant body he feels pleasure;
sbh1.3:18.9: for one at ease the mind is concentrated;
sbh1.3:18.10: with concentrated mind he knows as it actually is,
sbh1.3:18.12: knowing-and-seeing as it actually is, he becomes disenchanted;
sbh1.3:18.13: disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; dispassionate, he is liberated; for one liberated, the knowing-and-seeing of liberation arises;
sbh1.3:18.14: [and so on] up through: he attains final nirvāṇa in the nirvāṇa-element without remainder.
sbh1.3:18.15: [Thus] a virtuous individual, through the power of the purity of virtue, gains non-regret,
sbh1.3:18.16: and by gradual progression [proceeds] up to the going to nirvāṇa — this is the first benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:18.17: [2] Further, a virtuous individual, when the time of death is present, [reflects]: ‘good has been done by me, well [done] [Lacuna]; good conduct of body, speech, [and] mind [has been done by me]; bad conduct of body [etc.] has not been done by me,’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:18.19: of those who have done merit, done wholesome deeds, made a shelter against fear — to that destiny shall I, after death, go.’ He gains this second [kind of] non-regret,
sbh1.3:18.20: [which leads] to a happy destiny. For a non-regretful individual, death is good,
sbh1.3:18.21: the time of death is good, the after-state is good.
sbh1.3:18.22: This is the second benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:19.1: [3] Further, of the virtuous individual, fair praise, fame, renown, [and] report go forth.
sbh1.3:19.2: This is the third benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:20.1: [4] Further, the virtuous individual sleeps comfortably and [Conjectural: wakes] comfortably,
sbh1.3:20.2: with body and mind free from burning. This is the fourth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:20.3: [5] Further, the virtuous individual, even when asleep, is guarded by the deities.
sbh1.3:20.4: This is the fifth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:21.1: [6] Further, the virtuous individual is not apprehensive
sbh1.3:21.2: of harm from others, is not afraid, not of terrified mind.
sbh1.3:21.3: This is the sixth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:22.1: [7] Further, the virtuous individual — even when killers, enemies, [Damaged] have found an opening — is guarded;
sbh1.3:22.2: knowing always ‘this individual is such [a virtuous one],’ they fall either into friendship with him or into a neutral disposition.
sbh1.3:22.3: This is the seventh benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:23.1: [8] Further, even when [Damaged], yakṣas, resident spirits, [and] non-humans have found an opening, he is guarded —
sbh1.3:23.2: namely, by making that very virtue predominant.
sbh1.3:23.3: This is the eighth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:24.1: [9] Further, the virtuous individual, by Dharma [and] with little hardship, gains from others
sbh1.3:24.2: robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites — that is, on account of virtue, he is honored
sbh1.3:24.3: [and] esteemed by kings, royal ministers, townsmen, country-folk, the wealthy, the guild-masters, [and] caravan leaders.
sbh1.3:24.4: This is the ninth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:25.1: [10] Further, [as] above, all his aspirations succeed.
sbh1.3:25.2: If he wishes, [saying]: ‘In the realm of desire, may I be born in the company of kṣatriya families of great wealth, or brāhmaṇa families of great wealth, or householder families of great wealth, or among the deities of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṁśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, or Paranirmitavaśavartin’ — that [comes about] through the purity of his virtue, [Damaged]. ‘And may I, entering the dhyānas, dwell at ease in the visible-here-and-now,
sbh1.3:25.3: and may I be born in the company of the form-realm deities and dwell [there]’ — this aspiration of the virtuous, dispassionate one succeeds.
sbh1.3:25.5: ‘[Damaged] the liberations (*vimokṣa*) [Damaged] may I attain and dwell [in them]’;
sbh1.3:25.6: or ‘in the company of the formless-realm deities may I be born,’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:26.1: If he wishes, ‘may I attain nirvāṇa as the ultimate end,’ he attains [it].
sbh1.3:27.1: That [comes about] through the purity of his virtue and because he is everywhere dispassionate.
sbh1.3:27.2: This is to be understood as the tenth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:28.1: [Thus] the virtue-aggregate has been set forth by [its] division; the ruin and the fullness [of virtue] have been set forth;
sbh1.3:28.2: the synonyms have been set forth;
sbh1.3:28.3: the review constituting purification has been set forth, [and] the benefit has been set forth.
sbh1.3:29.1: This wholly complete restraint of virtue, included among the requisites, has been declared, set forth, opened up, [and] made manifest — in it sons of good family, desirous of their own good and of asceticism and brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*), should train.
sbh1.3:31.1: The division is to be known as threefold, the fullness as tenfold,
sbh1.3:31.2: the synonyms as six-fold; the purification is held as threefold,
sbh1.3:31.3: the benefit as tenfold — such is the restraint of virtue.
sbh1.3:32.1: What is restraint of the senses?
sbh1.3:32.2: When someone here dwells with guarded sense-doors, of guarded mindfulness, of alert mindfulness — [as elaborated] in detail.
sbh1.3:32.3: How, then, does he dwell with guarded sense-doors? He is of guarded mindfulness,
sbh1.3:32.4: of alert mindfulness — [as elaborated] in detail, up to: he guards the mind-faculty; over the mind-faculty
sbh1.3:32.6: Thus he dwells with guarded sense-doors.
sbh1.3:32.7: How, then, is his mindfulness guarded?
sbh1.3:32.8: When someone here, taking the very [practice of] guarded sense-doors as predominant, holds firmly to what has been heard,
sbh1.3:32.10: And by that, he attains a mindfulness whose predominant ground is hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
sbh1.3:32.11: Of that mindfulness once attained — so that it is not forgotten, is realized, is not lost — he applies effort and practice, from time to time, on that same teaching he heard, and he applies effort and practice in reflecting on it and cultivating it.
sbh1.3:32.12: He does not let his application drop. Thus, of the mindfulness born from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, the guarding is performed from time to time through the practice of those very three.
sbh1.3:32.13: Thus he becomes one of guarded mindfulness.
sbh1.3:32.14: How does he have alert mindfulness?
sbh1.3:32.15: He becomes one constantly active in that very mindfulness.
sbh1.3:32.17: Of these, constant action (*nityakāritā*) is what is called continual action (*sātatyakāritā*).
sbh1.3:32.18: Action toward going-forth (*niryāṇakāritā*) is what is called earnest action (*satkṛtyakāritā*).
sbh1.3:32.19: He who acts thus — continually and in earnest — is called one of alert mindfulness.
sbh1.3:32.21: so he does not lose that mindfulness;
sbh1.3:32.23: so in that very unlost mindfulness he gains strength,
sbh1.3:32.24: by which he becomes able and fit for the overcoming of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, dharmas.
sbh1.3:32.25: How is his mind guarded by mindfulness?
sbh1.3:32.26: Depending on the eye and forms, there arises
sbh1.3:32.27: eye-consciousness; immediately after eye-consciousness there arises
sbh1.3:32.28: discriminative mind-consciousness; by that discriminative mind-consciousness, one is drawn toward pleasing forms
sbh1.3:32.29: and feels ill will toward displeasing forms.
sbh1.3:32.30: Taking that very [mindfulness] as predominant, he guards [the mind] against the unwise discrimination that produces defilement,
sbh1.3:32.31: so that defilement does not arise.
sbh1.3:32.32: Likewise for ear, nose, tongue, [and] body; and depending on mind and dharmas, mind-consciousness arises.
sbh1.3:32.33: And that mind-consciousness, accompanied by unwise discrimination, produces defilement,
sbh1.3:32.34: by which one is drawn toward pleasing dharmas
sbh1.3:32.35: and feels ill will toward displeasing dharmas.
sbh1.3:32.36: He guards that mental state against the unwise discrimination that produces defilement — and thus defilement does not arise in him.
sbh1.3:32.37: Thus he becomes one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness.
sbh1.3:32.38: How is he one who maintains a balanced state?
sbh1.3:32.41: Having guarded that mental state from the unwise discrimination that produces defilement, he settles it in wholesome equanimity or in indeterminate equanimity.
sbh1.3:32.42: Therefore he is called one who maintains a balanced state.
sbh1.3:32.43: Thus he becomes one who maintains a balanced state.
sbh1.3:32.44: And how, again, does he guard the mental state from the unwise discrimination that produces defilement?
sbh1.3:32.45: He does not become a seizer of signs.
sbh1.3:32.46: In those forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas he does not become a seizer of secondary features — that on account of which evil unwholesome dharmas would flow into his mind.
sbh1.3:32.47: If, even so, through lapse of mindfulness or through the strength of his defilements, even while he avoids sign-seizing and secondary-feature-seizing, there do arise
sbh1.3:32.48: evil unwholesome dharmas, [and,] ill-grasped, they do flow into the mind —
sbh1.3:32.49: he applies himself to their restraint.
sbh1.3:32.50: By these two modes, the mental state is guarded from the unwise discrimination that produces defilement.
sbh1.3:33.1: And how, having guarded the mental state by these two modes, does he settle it in wholesome or indeterminate equanimity?
sbh1.3:33.4: As it is said: ‘he guards the eye-faculty, undertakes restraint over the eye-faculty,’
sbh1.3:33.5: and just as ‘he guards the eye-faculty, undertakes restraint over the eye-faculty,’
sbh1.3:33.6: so for the ear, nose, tongue, and body — and he guards the mind-faculty, undertakes restraint over the mind-faculty.
sbh1.3:33.7: By these two modes, he settles that mental state in wholesome or indeterminate equanimity.
sbh1.3:34.1: How, with respect to the forms cognizable by the eye, does he not become a seizer of signs?
sbh1.3:34.3: of the form which is the range of eye-consciousness, becoming a seizer of that range
sbh1.3:34.5: That is what it means to become a seizer of signs.
sbh1.3:34.6: Namely, in forms cognizable by the eye, and likewise in dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
sbh1.3:34.7: If, then, he avoids that range —
sbh1.3:34.8: [the range] of eye-consciousness too — he does not become a seizer of signs
sbh1.3:34.9: in forms cognizable by the eye, and likewise in dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness.
sbh1.3:34.10: How does he not become a seizer of secondary features?
sbh1.3:34.11: [That is, with respect to] forms cognizable by the eye.
sbh1.3:34.13: in those very forms cognizable by the eye, the range of the discriminative mind-consciousness that arises immediately along with eye-consciousness — when [that range tends] toward lust, toward hatred, or toward delusion — he avoids that range,
sbh1.3:34.14: does not produce, with that object,
sbh1.3:34.15: that mind-consciousness — and thus he does not become a seizer of secondary features
sbh1.3:34.16: in forms cognizable by the eye,
sbh1.3:34.17: or in dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Another kind of sign-seizing and secondary-feature-seizing:
sbh1.3:34.18: Here, sign-seizing is when, having brought to presence the attention born from them, he sees with the eye the forms that have come into view.
sbh1.3:34.19: And the seizing of secondary features [proceeds as follows]:
sbh1.3:34.20: Those same forms that have come into the eye’s view: having brought to presence the attention born from them, he sees them,
sbh1.3:34.21: but [has] previously heard from another, by report:
sbh1.3:34.22: ‘There are such-and-such eye-cognizable forms’ — and the names, words, and letters that follow upon those [reports], making them predominant, relying on them, established in them, this person discriminates the eye-cognizable forms in accord with what he has heard. This is called
sbh1.3:34.24: As with eye-cognizable forms, so it is to be understood with dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, mind.
sbh1.3:34.25: This sign-seizing and secondary-feature-seizing: there is [that] on account of which, with respect to which, and under whose predominance his evil unwholesome dharmas flow into the mind,
sbh1.3:34.26: and there is [that] on account of which, with respect to which, and under whose predominance evil unwholesome dharmas [Conjectural: do not] flow into the mind.
sbh1.3:34.27: Of these, the sign-seizing, the secondary-feature-seizing, the unwise seizing — that which is the cause, the occasion, the predominant condition for his evil unwholesome dharmas to flow into the mind:
sbh1.3:34.28: that very form of sign-seizing and secondary-feature-seizing he avoids.
sbh1.3:34.30: Lust, and the bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct produced by lust;
sbh1.3:34.32: and the bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct produced by [Conjectural: hatred and] delusion — these are called evil unwholesome dharmas.
sbh1.3:34.33: How do they ‘flow into the mind’?
sbh1.3:34.34: With whatever object mind, mentation, [and] consciousness arise —
sbh1.3:34.36: Associated with mind, mentation, [and] consciousness that have that object, the bodily-, verbal-, and mental-misconduct-producing lust, hatred, and delusion arise, go, follow along.
sbh1.3:34.37: Therefore they are said to ‘flow into the mind.’
sbh1.3:35.1: Thus, the defilement that would arise — through sign-seizing or secondary-feature-seizing — in eye-cognizable forms (and so on up to mind-cognizable dharmas) does not arise for one who avoids sign-seizing and secondary-feature-seizing.
sbh1.3:35.2: If, even so, through lapse of mindfulness or through the strength of his defilements, evil unwholesome dharmas arise even while he is dwelling alone — taking previously seen eye-cognizable forms as predominant, or taking previously experienced dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as predominant — once they have arisen he [Conjectural: does not accommodate] them, abandons them, purifies them, and puts an end to them.
sbh1.3:35.3: Therefore he is said to apply himself to their restraint.
sbh1.3:35.4: On forms toward which the eye is [properly] to be directed,
sbh1.3:35.5: and on dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind toward which the mind is [properly] to be directed,
sbh1.3:35.7: in such a way that he is not defiled.
sbh1.3:35.8: Thus the mind-faculty is guarded by him from that defilement.
sbh1.3:35.9: Therefore it is said: ‘he guards the mind-faculty.’
sbh1.3:35.10: On forms cognizable by the eye toward which the eye-faculty is not to be directed,
sbh1.3:35.11: and on dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind toward which the mind-faculty is not to be directed —
sbh1.3:35.12: to those he does not direct [his faculties] at all, in any way.
sbh1.3:35.13: Therefore it is said: ‘he undertakes restraint over the eye-faculty,’
sbh1.3:35.14: and so on up through ‘he undertakes restraint over the mind-faculty.’
sbh1.3:35.15: This much is the detailed exposition of sense-restraint, to be understood.
sbh1.3:35.17: by what one restrains, [Lacuna] from what one restrains, how one restrains, and what the restraint itself is —
sbh1.3:35.18: all this gathered into one is called restraint of the senses.
sbh1.3:35.20: By guarded mindfulness — by that he restrains.
sbh1.3:35.23: he restrains the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-faculty.
sbh1.3:35.26: From pleasing and displeasing forms, sounds, and so on up through dharmas — from these he restrains.
sbh1.3:35.28: He does not become a seizer of signs, does not become a seizer of secondary features — that on account of which evil unwholesome dharmas flow into the mind, to their restraint he applies himself; he guards the faculty, undertakes restraint over the faculty.
sbh1.3:35.30: And what is the restraint itself?
sbh1.3:35.31: That by which he is one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness,
sbh1.3:35.32: and one who maintains a balanced state —
sbh1.3:35.36: the object to be restrained, and the restraint itself —
sbh1.3:35.37: these gathered into one are called restraint of the senses.
sbh1.3:35.38: What is the means of restraint?
sbh1.3:35.39: What is said as: ‘he becomes one of guarded mindfulness, alert mindfulness; seeing forms with the eye, he does not become a seizer of signs, does not become a seizer of secondary features — up through: cognizing dharmas with the mind, he does not become a seizer of signs, does not become a seizer of secondary features’ —
sbh1.3:35.40: ‘that on account of which evil unwholesome dharmas would flow into the mind,
sbh1.3:35.41: to their restraint he applies himself;
sbh1.3:35.42: he guards the faculty, undertakes restraint over the faculty.’
sbh1.3:35.43: This is called the means of restraint.
sbh1.3:35.44: What is the object to be restrained?
sbh1.3:35.45: Eye-and-form, and so on up through mind-and-dharmas — this is called the object to be restrained.
sbh1.3:35.46: And what is the restraint itself?
sbh1.3:35.48: ‘he is one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness,
sbh1.3:35.49: one who maintains a balanced state’ — this is called restraint.
sbh1.3:35.50: This restraint of the senses is, in brief, of two kinds:
sbh1.3:35.51: that grounded in the power of reflection (*pratisaṁkhyāna-bala*), and that grounded in the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*).
sbh1.3:35.52: Of these, the one grounded in the power of reflection is that by which he sees danger in the sense-objects,
sbh1.3:35.53: but does not remove that danger,
sbh1.3:35.55: The one grounded in the power of cultivation is that by which he sees danger in the sense-objects and also removes that danger,
sbh1.3:35.57: By sense-restraint grounded in the power of reflection, the obsession of defilement that takes sense-objects as its object does not arise, does not come to manifest —
sbh1.3:35.58: but he does not abandon, does not eradicate, the latent tendency settled in the basis.
sbh1.3:35.59: By sense-restraint grounded in the power of cultivation, the obsession of defilement that takes sense-objects as its object does not arise, does not come to manifest —
sbh1.3:35.60: and at all times he also abandons the latent tendency settled in the basis,
sbh1.3:35.62: This is the distinction; this is the import.
sbh1.3:35.63: This is the difference between sense-restraint grounded in the power of reflection and that grounded in the power of cultivation.
sbh1.3:35.64: The sense-restraint grounded in the power of reflection belongs to the path of requisites (*saṁbhāra-mārga*).
sbh1.3:35.65: The sense-restraint grounded in the power of cultivation
sbh1.3:35.66: is to be understood as falling within the plane of dispassion.
sbh1.3:36.1: What is knowing the right measure in food?
sbh1.3:36.2: When someone here takes food with [proper] reflection —
sbh1.3:36.3: not for frivolity, not for adornment, not for embellishment, [as elaborated] above.
sbh1.3:36.4: How does he take food with [proper] reflection?
sbh1.3:36.5: ‘Reflection’ here refers to that wisdom by which he sees the danger in morsel-made food and, having found it loathsome through seeing the danger, eats.
sbh1.3:37.2: [It is the danger seen] in that very morsel-made food, as connected with consumption, with transformation, or with seeking.
sbh1.3:37.3: What is the danger connected with consumption [in food]?
sbh1.3:37.4: When someone here, at the time of taking food endowed with color, endowed with smell, endowed with taste, very fine —
sbh1.3:37.5: when his morsel-food, as soon as it is put into the mouth, is ground by the mill of the teeth, soaked by the spreading saliva,
sbh1.3:37.7: at the time when it has rolled down through the throat-tube,
sbh1.3:37.8: it wholly, entirely loses that former, original agreeableness,
sbh1.3:37.10: and in that transformation underway, it appears like vomit.
sbh1.3:37.11: And [as for] that very state — if the consumer-individual were to attend to its appearance, to recollect it, his desire to enjoy [it] would in no way remain, [not] even with respect to other, as yet untransformed fine food.
sbh1.3:37.12: What more is to be said of that [later] state? By these manifold modes, by this sequence, with food-consumption as the predominant [factor], this fine appearance vanishes, and the danger appears, counted among the unclean.
sbh1.3:37.16: What is the transformation-connected danger in food?
sbh1.3:37.17: When he has taken that food and is satisfied, [and] when it undergoes transformation — in the middle watch of the night or in the last watch — it then [produces] blood, flesh, sinew, bone, skin and so on, of many kinds and many sorts:
sbh1.3:37.18: the impure substances in this body it increases and generates.

sbh1.3:42.30: Obscuring dharmas are those dharmas that occasion the hindrances and conduce to them. And what are they?
sbh1.3:42.31: Sense-desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, doubt; [Conjectural: attractiveness], the sign of aversion, darkness, thoughts of kin, of country and of not-dying, recollection of past laughter, play, delight and company; and the three times —
sbh1.3:42.32: [that is,] unwise dharma-reflection that pertains to the three times.
sbh1.3:42.33: From these, how, by walking, does he purify the mind?
sbh1.3:42.34: [And] from how many [does he so purify it]?
sbh1.3:42.35: From sloth-and-torpor and from the [other] obscuration that is the food of sloth-and-torpor he purifies [the mind].
sbh1.3:42.36: The light-sign (*ālokanimitta*) is by him well, thoroughly grasped,
sbh1.3:42.39: He, with mind accompanied by light, accompanied by radiance — under cover or in the open, while walking on the walking-path — by some gladdening object instructs the mind,
sbh1.3:42.42: namely, by recollection of the Buddha, or of the Dharma, the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity or the deities.
sbh1.3:42.43: Or [he draws on] those dharmas which he has heard, grasped, [and] retained that concern the danger of sloth-and-torpor —
sbh1.3:42.44: namely: sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhuta-dharma, [and] upadeśa — wherein, in many ways, sloth-and-torpor is censured and deplored,
sbh1.3:42.47: Those [passages] he recites aloud in a full voice,
sbh1.3:42.48: or he proclaims them to others, or reflects on their meaning,
sbh1.3:42.49: weighs them, examines them; or he gazes around at the directions,
sbh1.3:42.50: or holds his gaze on the [Conjectural: moon], the constellations, the planets and the stars, [or] wets his face with water.
sbh1.3:42.51: Thus his obsession by sloth-and-torpor, when unarisen, does not arise; and when arisen, departs. Thus by him the mind is purified of that obscuring dharma.
sbh1.3:42.52: By sitting, from which obscuring dharmas does he purify the mind?
sbh1.3:42.53: From sense-desire, ill-will, restlessness-and-regret, doubt, and the [other] dharmas that feed them.
sbh1.3:42.54: When the obsession of sense-desire has arisen, for its dispelling — or when it has not arisen, for keeping it far off — sitting cross-legged, having set the body upright, having established mindfulness to the fore, he attends to the discolored, the festering, [Conjectural: the decomposed], the swollen, the gnawed, the bloodied, the bone, the skeleton, or some other excellent sign of concentration;
sbh1.3:42.55: or [he draws on] those dharmas which, [touching on] the abandonment of sense-lust itself, have been grasped for the abandonment of sense-lust,
sbh1.3:42.56: retained, mastered by voice, examined by mind, well penetrated by view — namely sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, [as elaborated] above:
sbh1.3:42.57: those [passages] which in many ways censure and depreciate sense-lust, sense-desire, sensual attachment, sensual compulsion, sensual fixation,
sbh1.3:42.59: and praise the abandonment of sense-lust in many ways,
sbh1.3:42.61: To those very dharmas — sitting thus — he attends wisely; thus his unarisen sense-desire-obsession does not arise,

sbh1.3:42.65: Likewise the second, the third, the fourth — upward, downward, sideways, the entire endless world — [Conjectural: pervading] it, he attains and dwells.

sbh1.3:42.90: only cause, only effect; he does not superimpose what does not exist,
sbh1.3:42.91: [and] does not destroy what does exist, does not depreciate [it].
sbh1.3:42.92: He knows the actual as actual,
sbh1.3:42.93: namely as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self — [seeing] impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self dharmas [as such]. He, thus wisely attending, is without doubt and without indecision about the Buddha,
sbh1.3:42.94: [without doubt] about the Dharma, the Saṅgha, suffering, origin, cessation, path, cause, [and] about the dharmas arisen from causes — without doubt,
sbh1.3:42.96: The rest [is to be understood] as above.
sbh1.3:42.97: Now, regarding ill-will, it should be said:

sbh1.3:42.99: regarding restlessness-and-regret, it should be said:
sbh1.3:42.100: the dharmas grasped, with respect to restlessness-and-regret, and for its abandonment, [as elaborated] above;
sbh1.3:42.101: regarding doubt, it should be said:

sbh1.3:42.103: and of the obscuring dharmas that are their food. Therefore he says: ‘by walking and sitting he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas.’
sbh1.3:42.104: And this is the purification of the mind from obscuring dharmas with the Dharma as the authority.
sbh1.3:42.105: There is also purification of the mind from obscuring dharmas with oneself as the authority, and with the world as the authority.
sbh1.3:42.106: What is that with oneself as the authority?
sbh1.3:42.107: When, on the arising of some particular hindrance, knowing by himself its [Conjectural: unsuitability], he does not accommodate the arisen hindrance —
sbh1.3:42.108: he abandons, dispels, puts an end to [it],
sbh1.3:42.109: not letting himself be marked by that hindrance, which defiles the mind, weakens wisdom and belongs to the side of ruin — thus, making himself the authority, he purifies the mind from the obscuring dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.110: How, making the world the authority, does he purify the mind from obscuring dharmas?
sbh1.3:42.111: Here, when a hindrance has arisen for him, or its time of arising is present,
sbh1.3:42.112: it occurs to him: ‘If I should produce an unarisen hindrance, the Teacher would reproach me, and the deities, the wise, [and] my co-religionists would censure me, regarding [it] as non-Dharma.’
sbh1.3:42.113: [Thus,] making the world the authority, he purifies the mind from the obscuring dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.117: He, making the world the authority, does not produce an unarisen hindrance, and abandons one that has arisen. Thus, making the world the authority, he purifies the mind from obscuring dharmas. For the sake of guarding his lodging, and [thinking] ‘I shall conform to worldly custom’, through the first watch of the night, by walking and sitting, he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.118: Having purified the mind of obscuring dharmas, washing his feet outside the dwelling,
sbh1.3:42.119: [and] having washed, entering the dwelling, he lies down —
sbh1.3:42.120: only for the building up of his own nourishment-born great elements, [thinking]:
sbh1.3:42.121: ‘This body, when [thus] replenished, will be more workable
sbh1.3:42.122: and more amenable in the continuous, [Damaged] application to the wholesome.’
sbh1.3:42.123: For what reason does he lie down on [his right] side?
sbh1.3:42.124: Because it shares a nature with the lion.
sbh1.3:42.126: The lion, among all animals of the animal-womb, is the boldest, the most enthusiastic, of firm valor.
sbh1.3:42.127: The monk too, applied to wakefulness, with aroused energy, dwells
sbh1.3:42.129: Hence for him the lion-couch is appropriate — not the ghost-couch, the deity-couch, nor the sense-pleasure-enjoyer’s couch —
sbh1.3:42.130: for they [whose couches those are] are all indolent, of low vigor, of feeble strength and valor.
sbh1.3:42.131: Moreover, it is the nature of things that for one who lies down on the right side in lion-fashion the limbs do not toss about so,
sbh1.3:42.132: no forgetfulness of mindfulness for one [thus] sleeping,
sbh1.3:42.133: and he does not sleep deeply,
sbh1.3:42.134: and he does not see evil dreams.
sbh1.3:42.135: For one who lies down otherwise, the contrary faults are to be understood.
sbh1.3:42.136: Therefore he says: ‘he lies down on the right side.’
sbh1.3:42.137: The light-sign is by him well grasped,
sbh1.3:42.140: Just attending to it, with mind accompanied by light, he lies down,
sbh1.3:42.141: and for him, even sleeping, the mind does not enter a
sbh1.3:42.142: darkened state. Thus, perceiving light, he lies down.
sbh1.3:42.143: How, mindful, does he lie down?
sbh1.3:42.145: reflected on, cultivated, wholesome, conducive to benefit — the mindfulness that follows on them continues until the time of sleep,
sbh1.3:42.146: so that those very dharmas present themselves to him asleep as when awake, and the mind moves abundantly in those very dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.147: Thus, according to his mindfulness, as he is mindful,
sbh1.3:42.148: he lies down with a wholesome mind,
sbh1.3:42.151: How, fully aware, does he lie down?
sbh1.3:42.152: For him, sleeping thus mindfully, when at any time, by some secondary defilement, mental defilement occurs,
sbh1.3:42.153: of that arising defilement he is rightly fully aware; he does not accommodate, he abandons, he penetrates [it],
sbh1.3:42.154: he turns the mind back [from it].
sbh1.3:42.155: Therefore he is said to lie down fully aware.
sbh1.3:42.156: How, attending to the perception of rising, does he lie down?
sbh1.3:42.157: He lies down having made the mind held [steady] by energy,
sbh1.3:42.158: with [a disposition to] easy waking, with a well-gladdened mind, just like a forest deer;
sbh1.3:42.159: he does not let the mind wholly, entirely incline toward the onset of sleep,
sbh1.3:42.163: ‘Oh, may I in every respect, in every way, accomplish the wakefulness authorized by the Buddhas!’
sbh1.3:42.164: And for its accomplishment he dwells with longing, relish, application and desire, and is applied.
sbh1.3:42.166: ‘Just as today, for the sake of wakefulness with aroused energy, I have dwelt — and, for the cultivation of wholesome dharmas, skilled, not lazy, endowed with exertion — tomorrow at dawn, when night has gone forth, in still greater measure I shall dwell with aroused energy, endowed with exertion.’
sbh1.3:42.167: Now, by [the first kind of] rising-perception he [Conjectural: does not] sleep deeply,
sbh1.3:42.168: by which he is able to rise quickly, very quickly at rising-time — not waking after the time has passed.
sbh1.3:42.169: By the second [kind of] rising-perception, he arranges the lion-couch authorized by the Buddhas, neither subtracting nor adding [from it].
sbh1.3:42.170: By the third [kind of] rising-perception, the desire [for wakefulness-yoga] he does not let slacken.
sbh1.3:42.171: When forgetfulness arises, in each subsequent moment he applies himself to renewed undertaking.
sbh1.3:42.172: Thus, attending to the rising-perception, he lies down.
sbh1.3:42.173: He, in the last watch of the night, waking quickly, very quickly, purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.175: means the late night, a watch and more.
sbh1.3:42.177: fully aware, attending to the perception of rising, having slept through the middle watch, a watch and more, at whatever time he rises,
sbh1.3:42.178: at that time he rises up,
sbh1.3:42.180: Having risen, not overcome by strong sloth-and-torpor obsession,
sbh1.3:42.181: by which there would be in his rising slowness, sluggishness, [or] laziness and indolence;
sbh1.3:42.182: rather, in the absence of that slowness, sluggishness, laziness and indolence, his rising is quick, very quick, at a mere turn of attention, without having to struggle. The purification from the obscuring dharmas is to be understood as above.
sbh1.3:42.183: This much is the detailed division of application to wakefulness in the early and late watches of the night.
sbh1.3:42.185: Here, for the person applied to wakefulness-yoga, there are four right tasks.
sbh1.3:42.187: As long as he is awake, he does not let go of the wholesome side,
sbh1.3:42.188: [remaining] in continuous, [Damaged] cultivation of wholesome dharmas; and at the [proper] time he lies down,
sbh1.3:42.190: and he goes to sleep with an undefiled mind,
sbh1.3:42.192: and at the [proper] time he wakes,
sbh1.3:42.194: With reference to these four right tasks, the application to wakefulness has been taught by the Blessed One to the disciples.
sbh1.3:42.197: ‘by day, by walking and sitting, he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas;
sbh1.3:42.198: thus in the first watch of the night,’ by this the first right task is declared,
sbh1.3:42.199: namely: as long as he is awake, he does not let go of the wholesome side,
sbh1.3:42.200: [remaining] in continuous, [Damaged] cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.202: ‘washing the feet outside the dwelling, entering the dwelling, he lies down on the right side,
sbh1.3:42.203: foot placed on foot,’ by this the second right task is declared,
sbh1.3:42.204: namely: at the [proper] time he lies down,
sbh1.3:42.208: fully aware, attending to the perception of rising, he lies down,’ by this the third right task is declared,
sbh1.3:42.209: namely: he goes to sleep with an undefiled mind,
sbh1.3:42.211: When he then says: ‘in the last watch of the night, waking quickly, very quickly, he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas,’ by this the fourth right task is declared,
sbh1.3:42.212: namely: at the [proper] time he wakes,
sbh1.3:42.214: Thus where it is said ‘perceiving light, mindful, fully aware, attending to the rising-perception, he lies down,’
sbh1.3:42.215: from [these] two causes he goes to sleep with an undefiled mind —
sbh1.3:42.216: namely, by mindfulness and full awareness; [and] from two further causes he wakes in time,
sbh1.3:42.218: namely, by perception of light and perception of rising.
sbh1.3:42.219: How so? He goes to sleep having taken hold of a wholesome object;
sbh1.3:42.220: and by full awareness he quickly, very quickly knows rightly the mind that is falling away from that wholesome object and becoming defiled.
sbh1.3:42.221: Thus by these two causes his sleep is undefiled.
sbh1.3:42.222: And by perception of light and perception of rising,
sbh1.3:42.224: [and] his torpor-obsession does not become far-going.
sbh1.3:42.225: Thus by these two causes he wakes in time,
sbh1.3:42.227: This, then, is the summary meaning of application to wakefulness:
sbh1.3:42.228: [the preceding] detailed analysis, and this summary meaning.
sbh1.3:42.229: This is called application to wakefulness in the early and late watches of the night.
