sbh1.3:47.9: this is called for him going.
sbh1.3:47.10: When someone here stands on the walking-path, or stands in front of co-religionists,
sbh1.3:47.11: preceptors, instructors, gurus, [or] persons occupying the place of guru — this is called standing.
sbh1.3:47.12: When someone here sits or settles on a couch, stool, [or] grass-mat,
sbh1.3:47.13: folding the legs cross-wise, having set the body upright, having established mindfulness to the fore — this is called
sbh1.3:47.15: When someone here, washing the feet outside the dwelling, entering the dwelling, lies down on the right side in lion-fashion,
sbh1.3:47.16: foot placed on foot, on couch, stool, or grass-mat, in forest, foot of tree, [or] empty hut —
sbh1.3:47.18: When someone here by day, by walking and sitting, purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas, [and] likewise in the first watch and the last watch of the night —
sbh1.3:47.20: When someone here, so applied to wakefulness, takes up [and]
sbh1.3:47.21: masters dharmas not yet taken up —
sbh1.3:47.24: and in the dharmas taken up he makes himself familiar by voice —
sbh1.3:47.25: namely, in detail, by recitation; or proclaims them to others in detail;
sbh1.3:47.27: [and] exchanges friendly speech with wise co-religionists, or with other [persons], householders, only so far as [serves] to encourage [them] and for the sake of requisites — this is called
sbh1.3:47.29: When someone here — of the dharmas heard, mastered, [and] mentally examined — alone, secluded, reflects on the meaning, weighs, examines [them];
sbh1.3:47.30: or, withdrawn, establishes the mind inwardly,
sbh1.3:47.36: or applies himself in yoga to *vipaśyanā* (insight) — this is called being silent.
sbh1.3:47.37: When someone here, when summer-time has come, in the burning heat of the hottest summer, is afflicted by heat,
sbh1.3:47.40: out-of-time sleep-fatigue, the desire to sleep —
sbh1.3:47.42: And he, regarding going and so on up through the dispelling of sleep-fatigue,
sbh1.3:47.43: rightly knows each by its specific characteristic;
sbh1.3:47.44: where one should go, [and so on] up to: where sleep-fatigue should be dispelled —
sbh1.3:47.46: when it should be gone to,
sbh1.3:47.47: [and so on] up to: when sleep-fatigue
sbh1.3:47.51: [and so on] up to: how sleep-fatigue
sbh1.3:47.52: should be dispelled — that too he rightly knows.
sbh1.3:47.53: This is called for him full awareness.
sbh1.3:47.54: He, endowed with that full awareness,
sbh1.3:47.55: going, [and so on] up to: dispelling sleep-fatigue, knows
sbh1.3:47.56: ‘I am going, [and so on] up to: I am dispelling sleep-fatigue’;
sbh1.3:47.58: and where the sleep-fatigue should be dispelled,
sbh1.3:47.66: he dispels the sleep-fatigue. This is called for him [Lacuna]
sbh1.3:48.1: What is the sequence of dwelling with full awareness, and what does it [Conjectural: bring out]? When someone here, depending on whichever village or market-town he dwells in,
sbh1.3:48.3: ‘This village or market-town is to be approached by me for alms.
sbh1.3:48.4: Having gone for alms, I should return again to the dwelling.
sbh1.3:48.6: in this village or town families that are not to be approached by me.
sbh1.3:48.9: a cowherd settlement, a tavern, a prostitute’s house, the royal household, a caṇḍāla quarter,
sbh1.3:48.10: or families wholly hostile [and] not to be won round.
sbh1.3:48.11: And there are families to be approached by me —
sbh1.3:48.12: namely, kṣatriya families of great wealth, brāhmaṇa families of great wealth, market-town families, country families, wealthy families, guild-master families, [and] caravan-leader families — [these] are to be approached, but not too late in the evening,
sbh1.3:48.13: not at the wrong time, not when the donor-patrons are busy with work, not when [they are] engaged in play or pleasure or adornment, not when engaged in sexual intercourse, not when angry.
sbh1.3:48.14: And I should approach in such a way that, approaching, I would not encounter a runaway elephant, a [Conjectural: runaway chariot], a fierce horse, a fierce cow, [or] a fierce dog; would not tread on dense undergrowth or thorny barricades,
sbh1.3:48.15: would not fall into a pit, a muddy pool, a precipice,
sbh1.3:48.16: not into refuse-water, not into cesspits. Like the moon I should approach the families,
sbh1.3:48.17: possessing moral shame, non-brazen, withdrawn in body, withdrawn in mind, not desiring gain, not desiring honor.
sbh1.3:48.18: As I am clear-minded [and] glad at my own gain, so I should be clear-minded [and] glad at another’s gain — non-self-aggrandizing, non-other-deprecating,
sbh1.3:48.19: of compassionate mind, of pitying mind.
sbh1.3:48.20: And thus again I should approach.
sbh1.3:48.21: For how could one gone forth expect this in others’ families: “Let others give to me, [Conjectural: and not withhold],” [and so on] up to “quickly, not slowly,” [as elaborated] in detail?’
sbh1.3:48.22: ‘Having approached, in receiving [I] should observe due measure,
sbh1.3:48.23: and not for the sake of gain should I make hypocrisy;
sbh1.3:48.24: talkative chatter, insinuation, extortion, gain-seeking-by-gain should not be made;
sbh1.3:48.25: and that gain should be enjoyed unattached, unclinging, ungreedy, unbinding, unbeguiled, unfixated, [and] not fallen into fixation.
sbh1.3:48.26: And [as for] those forms which in approaching or having approached are [normally] to be seen,
sbh1.3:48.27: only some of those are to be looked at;
sbh1.3:48.28: toward those not to be looked at, one should be with eyes averted,
sbh1.3:48.29: with well-collected senses; toward those that are [proper] to be seen, [one should be] with well-established mindfulness.
sbh1.3:48.30: What kind of forms are not to be looked at?
sbh1.3:48.31: Namely: a dancer, a comedian, a jester,
sbh1.3:48.32: or any other such [Conjectural: amusement] going on, in dance, song or music;
sbh1.3:48.33: likewise womankind, and in particular one young, of fine complexion, attractive — and [in general] those forms whose seeing would harm the holy life, would be an obstacle to the holy life, [or] would conduce to the manifestation of evil, unwholesome thoughts —
sbh1.3:48.34: such forms are not to be looked at ahead, nor looked around at. What kind of forms are to be seen?
sbh1.3:48.35: Namely: the aged, old, decrepit, of wheezing breath, of forward-bowed body, leaning on a staff, of trembling body; or one afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, with swollen feet, swollen hands, swollen belly, swollen face, pale, eczema-ridden, scabies-ridden, leprous, suffering, of struck-down limbs;
sbh1.3:48.36: of withered body, of impaired faculties;
sbh1.3:48.37: or [one] dead, time-gone, one-day dead, two-days dead, seven-days dead,
sbh1.3:48.38: devoured by crows, ospreys, vultures, dogs, [or] jackals, eaten by various animal-creatures; or [a corpse being] carried — placed on a bier with canopy spread above, with a great crowd in front and behind, weeping, lamenting, dust-strewn, with loosened hair, in sorrow, in suffering,
sbh1.3:48.40: in dejection, in distress — these are what should be seen; and other such forms are to be seen,
sbh1.3:48.41: [namely] those that conduce to the support of the holy life and to the manifestation of wholesome thoughts.
sbh1.3:48.42: One should not approach with shaking body, shaking arms, [or] shaking head; not laughing aloud; not arm-in-arm, not with shoulders shrugged; not without leave.
sbh1.3:48.43: One should not sit on a seat
sbh1.3:48.44: without examining the seat; not laying the whole body upon it, not [with] foot on foot, not [with] thigh on thigh, not [with] feet contracted, not [with] feet spread; not wrapped over the head, not lifted high, not spread wide, not hitched up — the robe put on all round, not too high, not too low, not [hanging] like an elephant’s trunk, not like a palmyra-fan, not like a nāga’s hood,
sbh1.3:48.45: nor worn like a lump of beans. One should not hold out the bowl before the food has come, nor should [it] be [Conjectural: held] over the chewable and edible food;
sbh1.3:48.46: one should not place the bowl on uncovered ground or in a precipitous, sloping place; the alms-food should be eaten in due order.
sbh1.3:48.47: One should not cover the soup with rice,
sbh1.3:48.48: nor the rice with soup; nor should one eat [Conjectural: greedily]; one should make a round morsel, not too large, not too small,
sbh1.3:48.49: not licking the hand, not licking the bowl,
sbh1.3:48.50: not shaking the hand, not shaking the bowl,
sbh1.3:48.51: not breaking [up] the morsel — [thus] alms-food should be eaten.
sbh1.3:49.1: ‘And when I have returned to the dwelling from those families, having come and again gone out, by day or by night, I should walk on a private walking-path,
sbh1.3:49.3: [nor on one] not entrusted, not permitted, not assigned [to him]; with body unfatigued, body unwearied, with mind restrained from agitation, applied to the wholesome side, [Conjectural: accompanied by attention], with faculties turned inward, with mind not going outward, not too swiftly, not too restlessly, not solely engaged in going-and-returning — going from time to time, standing from time to time. Thus in his own dwelling,
sbh1.3:49.4: in his own precinct, in his own hut, in [one] assigned [to him], in a private [one] — not in another’s, [nor in one] not entrusted, not permitted — thus on couch or stool or grass-mat, in forest or at the foot of a tree or [in an] empty hut, one should sit,
sbh1.3:49.5: folding the legs cross-wise, having set the body upright, having established mindfulness to the fore. In the middle watch of the night one should sleep,
sbh1.3:49.6: and the day and first watch [of the night] should be passed on the wholesome side,
sbh1.3:50.1: perceiving light, mindful, fully aware, attending to the perception of rising. In the last watch of the night, waking quickly, very quickly, application should be made to discussion or recitation,
sbh1.3:50.2: or to exertion, retreat, [or] dharma-reflection — and the Lokāyata texts should be avoided,
sbh1.3:50.3: [those] of ornate letters, ornate words and phrases, conducing to no good, which lead not to higher knowledge, not to awakening, not to nirvāṇa.
sbh1.3:50.4: Those dharmas, however, spoken by the Tathāgata, deep, of deep appearance, connected with emptiness, conforming to specific conditionality [and] dependent origination — those should be grasped in earnest,
sbh1.3:50.5: firmly, stably, well grasped, not destroyed,
sbh1.3:50.6: for the accomplishment of [meditative] practice, not for gain and honor;
sbh1.3:50.7: and those dharmas should be well mastered by voice.
sbh1.3:50.8: And one should not pass time in company, in love of work, in love of speech; from time to time, with mindfulness established, one should greet wise co-religionists, converse with them, [and] exchange friendly speech; and one should be of the inquiring sort, a seeker of what is wholesome,
sbh1.3:51.1: with a non-accusatory mind, of measured speech, of suitable speech, of calm speech.
sbh1.3:52.1: And having spoken a Dharma-talk to others, in silence [and] without desire, evil, unwholesome thoughts should not be thought,
sbh1.3:52.2: and one should not be applied to unwise dharma-reflection. [Lacuna]
sbh1.3:52.3: Thus many dharmas of this kind have been grasped by him,
sbh1.3:52.4: retained, well mastered by voice, examined by mind,
sbh1.3:52.7: How is he an attainer [of meditative states]?
sbh1.3:52.8: He becomes a gainer of the perception of impermanence, of the perception of suffering in the impermanent, of the perception of non-self in suffering, of the perception of food as repugnant, of the perception of the bloody, of the perception of the scattered, of the perception of the bone, [and] of the perception that reviews emptiness.
sbh1.3:52.10: of the first dhyāna, [the] second, third, [and] fourth; of the sphere of infinite space, of infinite consciousness, of nothingness, [and] of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; of loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, [and] sympathetic joy; of the fruit of stream-entry, of once-returning and of non-returning; of [Conjectural: the range of psychic power], of past abodes, of the divine ear, of decease-and-rebirth, of the ways of [others’] minds, of arhatship, [and] of meditation in the eight liberations.
sbh1.3:52.12: and competent to admonish others by the three wonders:
sbh1.3:52.13: the wonder of psychic power, the wonder of mind-reading, the wonder of admonition.
sbh1.3:52.16: Toward others he is full of compassion,
sbh1.3:52.17: full of pity, desirous of their welfare,
sbh1.3:52.18: desirous of their benefit, [their] ease, [their] comfort, [their] security from bondage.
sbh1.3:52.20: How is he of unwearying mind?
sbh1.3:52.22: an exhorter, an arouser, a gladdener, a knower of the four assemblies, skilled in Dharma-teaching, non-lazy, full of initiative,
sbh1.3:52.23: of aroused energy, of aroused-energy nature.
sbh1.3:52.24: Thus he is of unwearying mind.
sbh1.3:52.26: Abused, he does not abuse in return;
sbh1.3:52.27: angered [against], he does not anger in return;
sbh1.3:52.28: [Conjectural: struck, he does not strike back];
sbh1.3:52.29: [Conjectural: mocked, he does not mock in return].
sbh1.3:52.30: [Conjectural: he endures the stick]; even in tight bonds, imprisonment, beating, threatening, [or] cutting, he [counts] himself at fault,
sbh1.3:52.31: and has recourse to the ripening of [his own] action;
sbh1.3:52.32: he is not angry with others,
sbh1.3:52.33: nor does he bear a latent tendency [of anger].
sbh1.3:52.34: Thus disregarded, deprecated, [or] despised, he undergoes no change,
sbh1.3:52.35: intends nothing but [their] welfare — and he is patient
sbh1.3:52.36: of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, gnats, mosquitoes, wind, sun, [and] creeping things; of ill-spoken, ill-come [Conjectural: ways of speech] from others; of bodily feelings — painful, intense, harsh, sharp, disagreeable, life-threatening — he is patient, of accommodating nature.
sbh1.3:53.3: in an assembly he teaches Dharma
sbh1.3:53.4: with unfaltering voice, his mindfulness and ready speech unfailing;
sbh1.3:53.5: and fear arising from timidity does not arise in him, does not come upon him; nor does sweat run from his [Conjectural: armpits], [Damaged].
sbh1.3:53.7: How is he endowed with the speech-faculty?
sbh1.3:53.8: He is endowed with urbane, noble speech:
sbh1.3:53.9: sweet, distinct, intelligible, worth hearing, agreeable, independent, unlimited.
sbh1.3:53.10: Thus he is endowed with the speech-faculty,
sbh1.3:53.12: He, endowed with these eight causes, becomes an admonisher,
sbh1.3:53.13: a reminder, an advisor, an instructor, [and] a Dharma-teacher.
sbh1.3:54.2: Namely, he admonishes for a deficiency of virtue in higher virtue, for a deficiency of conduct in higher conduct, by what is seen, by what is heard, by what is suspected,
sbh1.3:54.3: by what is real, not by what is unreal; in [proper] time, not out of time; connected with meaning, not unconnected with meaning; gently, not harshly; with friendliness, not with hostility.
sbh1.3:54.6: He reminds [the other] of a transgression,
sbh1.3:54.7: or of the Dharma, or of its meaning.
sbh1.3:54.8: How does he remind of a transgression?
sbh1.3:54.9: When someone who has committed a transgression [Conjectural: does not] remember it,
sbh1.3:54.11: ‘Friend, in such a place, in such a matter, at such a time, you committed such-and-such [a transgression].’ Thus he reminds of the transgression.
sbh1.3:54.12: How does he remind of Dharma?
sbh1.3:54.13: When someone, alone, [tries to] recall the dharmas [previously] heard, grasped —
sbh1.3:54.15: namely sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, [as elaborated] above — [but] does not recall [them],
sbh1.3:54.18: or the asking-and-inquiring [that draws it out]. Thus he reminds of dharmas.
sbh1.3:54.19: How does he remind of the meaning of Dharma?
sbh1.3:54.25: and what is wholesome, connected with meaning, connected with the holy life,
sbh1.3:54.26: long since done, long since spoken — of that too he reminds.
sbh1.3:54.29: In seclusion, retreat, yoga, attention, [and] *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm and insight), from time to time he gives appropriate advice,
sbh1.3:54.30: and from time to time engages in connected talk —
sbh1.3:54.31: namely, agreeable talk leading to the mind’s freedom from hindrance: virtue-talk, wisdom-talk, liberation-talk, talk of few-desires, talk of the knowing-and-seeing of liberation, contentment-talk, abandonment-talk, dispassion-talk, cessation-talk, decrease-talk, non-mixing-talk, [and] talk in accord with dependent origination, with this-conditionality.
sbh1.3:54.34: By Dharma and Vinaya, in the dispensation of the Teacher who instructs — being a teacher (*ācārya*),
sbh1.3:54.35: or [being] a preceptor, or a co-religionist, or a guru, or a person occupying the place of a guru — in any matter of [the disciple’s] overstepping or transgression, knowing of it,
sbh1.3:54.36: from time to time he chastens [him],
sbh1.3:54.39: and again, by Dharma, once he has come to terms, he accepts his friendly service, his respectful conduct, and his understanding;
sbh1.3:54.40: and he is one who restores him;
sbh1.3:54.41: in what should be done and not done, [Damaged] in what he habitually practises and what he does not, he teaches and instructs. Thus he is an instructor.
sbh1.3:54.43: From time to time he gives the preliminary-action talk —
sbh1.3:54.44: namely, [the talks on] generosity, virtue, heaven, the danger in sense-pleasures, the escape, [and on] the dharmas on the side of purification, [all] of which he proclaims in detail.
sbh1.3:54.45: From time to time he gives talk connected with the four noble truths,
sbh1.3:54.46: [talk] taking up suffering, origin, cessation, [Conjectural: and the path] — for the maturation of beings, [Damaged] for the purification of beings, for the long endurance of the true Dharma — with suitable words and letters, coherent, conforming, fitting the occasion, apt, befitting, compliant, the limbs and requisites of the prudent [teacher]; and he gives that talk at the [proper] time,
sbh1.3:54.48: gladdening, pleasing, encouraging, not depressing — suitable, accompanied [appropriately], unscattered, in accord with Dharma, in accord with the assembly, of friendly mind, beneficial mind, compassionate mind,
sbh1.3:54.49: not depending on gain, honor, [or] praise; he [Conjectural: does not] exalt himself,
sbh1.3:54.50: [and] does not deprecate others. Thus he is a Dharma-teacher.
sbh1.3:54.51: He who is endowed with these eight factors
sbh1.3:54.52: and is thus from time to time an admonisher, reminder,
sbh1.3:54.53: advisor, [and] instructor — therefore he is called a good friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
sbh1.3:54.54: This much is the detailed division of association with good friends (*kalyāṇamitratā*).
sbh1.3:54.56: If this friend, helper, compassionate one is, from the start, desirous of [the disciple’s] welfare
sbh1.3:54.58: and knows that very welfare-and-ease as it actually is,
sbh1.3:54.59: [being] unperverted, of unperverted view, capable and skilled in means —
sbh1.3:54.60: namely, for the accomplishment of that welfare-and-ease, for its conferral — and is skilled, not lazy, full of initiative, of aroused-energy nature,
sbh1.3:54.61: namely, taking up that very conferral of welfare-and-ease,
sbh1.3:54.62: [then,] wholly perfect by these four causes,
sbh1.3:54.63: he is in brief to be understood as the good friend.
sbh1.3:54.64: And this is the summary meaning of association with good friends.
sbh1.3:55.1: What was previously [given as] the detailed division, and what [is here] the summary meaning — this is called association with good friends.
sbh1.3:56.1: What is hearing-and-reflection on the true dharma?
sbh1.3:56.2: By ‘true dharma’ is meant: that which has been declared by the Buddhas and the disciples of Buddhas, by the true, the rightly-gone, [and] the good persons —
sbh1.3:56.6: Namely sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, [and the rest of the twelve, as elaborated above].
sbh1.3:56.7: The twelvefold word-genre is called true dharma.
sbh1.3:56.9: Whatever talks were given by the Blessed One, here and there, with reference to those various trainees and their various conducts — talks connected with the aggregates, with the elements, with the sense-bases,
sbh1.3:56.10: with dependent origination, with food and truth, or with disciples, solitary buddhas, and tathāgatas;
sbh1.3:56.11: or connected with the foundations of mindfulness, the right exertions, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the awakening-factors, the factors of the path;
sbh1.3:56.12: or talks given on unattractiveness, on mindfulness of breathing, on the training, on the confidence born of understanding (*avetyaprasāda*) —
sbh1.3:56.13: those very talks, taken up by the compilers for the long endurance of the teaching and arranged in due order, joined in due order,
sbh1.3:56.14: with appropriate sequences of names, words, and letters — that is, in such a way as to indicate the relevant meanings, which are wholesome, meaningful, and [Conjectural: connected with the holy life] — these are called sūtra.
sbh1.3:56.16: [A discourse] at whose end and conclusion verses are sung, and any sūtra whose meaning needs drawing out (*neyārtha*) — this is called geya.
sbh1.3:56.18: [A discourse] in which, regarding disciples who have passed away, their [next] rebirth is predicted,
sbh1.3:56.19: together with sūtras whose meaning is final (*nītārtha*) — this is called
sbh1.3:56.22: What is not spoken in prose,
sbh1.3:56.23: but composed in lines — of two, three, four, five, or six lines — this is called gāthā.
sbh1.3:57.2: [A discourse] spoken by way of declaration, without announcing a person’s name and clan, for the future continuance of the true dharma and of the teaching.
sbh1.3:58.2: [A discourse] spoken by way of indication, with a person's name and lineage announced;
sbh1.3:58.3: and the vinaya-connected Prātimokṣa-sūtra with its origin and occasioning cause — this is called nidāna.
sbh1.3:58.6: by which parable the present matter is illuminated — this is called
sbh1.3:58.9: Whatever is connected with former lives (*pūrvayoga*) — this is called vṛttaka.
sbh1.3:59.2: Where the bodhisattva-conducts and difficult deeds of the Blessed One, in his successive births in the past, here and there,
sbh1.3:60.2: Where the bodhisattvas' path is taught —
sbh1.3:60.4: for the perfecting of the ten powers and the unobstructed knowledge —
sbh1.3:61.2: Where the special qualities of the Buddhas, the disciples of Buddhas, monks, nuns, female probationers, [Lacuna] female novices, [Lacuna] female lay-followers — shared and unshared, surpassing all others, held to be wondrous and marvelous — are declared, these are called wonderful dharmas.
sbh1.3:62.2: All the mātṛkās, the abhidharma, and the digests drawn from the sūtras.
sbh1.3:62.4: And of this twelvefold word-genre there is sūtra, there is vinaya, there is abhidharma.
sbh1.3:62.6: ‘sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, avadāna, vṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, wonderful dharmas’ —
sbh1.3:62.15: This twelvefold scripture, subsumed under the three baskets,
sbh1.3:62.16: taught by the true, the rightly-gone,
sbh1.3:62.18: And the hearing of it is
sbh1.3:62.19: the hearing of the true dharma.
sbh1.3:62.21: When someone here is a sūtra-bearer (*sūtra-dhara*),
sbh1.3:62.23: or a mātṛkā-bearer, or a sūtra-vinaya-bearer, or a sūtra-abhidharma-bearer, or a vinaya-mātṛkā-bearer —
sbh1.3:62.24: this is called hearing of the true dharma.
sbh1.3:62.27: hearing of the letter and hearing of the meaning.
sbh1.3:62.29: When someone here, alone and secluded, [takes up] those very dharmas as heard —
sbh1.3:62.30: having set aside the six matters that are unthinkable (namely: reflection on self, on the being, on the world, on the karmic-results of beings, on the meditators’ domain of meditation, and on the Buddhas’ domain of Buddhas) — he reflects on them by their own characteristic
sbh1.3:62.32: That reflection, again, is twofold: by way of enumeration (joined with the enumeration-procedure for dharma),
sbh1.3:62.33: and by way of weighing (by reasoning, examining merits and faults).
sbh1.3:62.34: Whether he reflects on the aggregate-connected teaching,
sbh1.3:62.35: or on any other teaching stated before, he reflects by these two.
sbh1.3:62.38: And that form included in the dharma-sense-base — that is the form-aggregate; the three feelings are the feeling-aggregate.
sbh1.3:62.39: The six perception-bodies are the perception-aggregate.
sbh1.3:62.40: The six volition-bodies are the [Conjectural: formations-aggregate].
sbh1.3:62.41: The six consciousness-bodies are the consciousness-aggregate. Thus, by way of enumeration-and-counting, he reflects on the aggregates with progressive subdivision; the entry-procedure for this enumeration-mode of reflection is to be understood as boundless.
sbh1.3:62.42: How does he reflect on the aggregate-teaching by way of examining reasoning?
sbh1.3:62.44: Which four? Namely: the reasoning of dependence, the reasoning of cause-and-effect, proof-establishing reasoning,
sbh1.3:63.1: What is the reasoning of dependence?
sbh1.3:63.2: Dependence is twofold: dependence-of-arising and dependence-of-designation.
sbh1.3:63.3: Of these, dependence-of-arising: the causes and conditions on which the manifestation of the aggregates depends.
sbh1.3:63.4: In that arising of the aggregates, those causes and conditions are depended upon.
sbh1.3:63.5: [Dependence-of-designation:] the sequences of names, words, and letters on which the designation of the aggregates depends.
sbh1.3:63.6: In that designation of the aggregates, those sequences of names, words, and letters are depended upon.
sbh1.3:63.7: This is called dependence-of-arising in the aggregates
sbh1.3:63.10: and whichever is the dependence-of-designation — that is the reasoning, the procedure, the means
sbh1.3:63.11: for the arising of the aggregates
sbh1.3:63.12: and for the designation of the aggregates; therefore it is called the reasoning of dependence.
sbh1.3:63.13: Reasoning of cause-and-effect: the engagement of the so-arisen aggregates, by means of their own cause and their own condition, in performing their respective proper functions — for example:
sbh1.3:63.14: by the eye, forms are to be seen;
sbh1.3:63.15: by the ear, sounds are to be heard;
sbh1.3:63.16: and so on up to: by the mind, dharmas are to be cognized.
sbh1.3:63.17: [Conversely:] form is to stand in the eye's range;
sbh1.3:63.18: sound in the ear's range; and so on through dharmas in the mind's range —
sbh1.3:63.19: and whatever else is of this kind.
sbh1.3:63.20: The reasoning, the procedure, the means in the respective effects and causes of this or that dharma — this is called
sbh1.3:63.23: [The propositions:] ‘the aggregates are impermanent, dependently arisen, suffering, empty, non-self’ — these he examines by three means of valid cognition: namely, reliable scripture, direct perception, and inference.
sbh1.3:63.24: By these three means of valid cognition, furnished with proof, which grip the hearts of the wise, delineation and establishment are made —
sbh1.3:63.25: namely, of the impermanence, dependent-arising, suffering, emptiness [Lacuna] of the aggregates. This is called proof-establishing reasoning.
sbh1.3:63.27: By what reason are these aggregates as they are, the world-arrangement as it is? By what reason is earth marked by hardness, water by fluidity, fire by heat, wind by motion?
sbh1.3:63.28: [By what reason are] the aggregates impermanent, [and] by what reason is nirvāṇa calm?
sbh1.3:63.29: [Likewise:] form is marked by being affected;
sbh1.3:63.30: feeling by experiencing, perception by recognizing, formations by forming, consciousness by cognizing.
sbh1.3:63.31: This is the nature of these dharmas; their own-nature is just this.
sbh1.3:63.32: This is the nature of things, and this very nature of things
sbh1.3:63.33: is the reasoning, the procedure, the means here.
sbh1.3:63.34: [Whether one asks:] Could this be so,
sbh1.3:63.35: or otherwise, or not at all — in every case the nature of things alone is the recourse; the nature of things alone is the reasoning,
sbh1.3:63.36: [It serves] for the mind to contemplate, for the mind to assent — this is called nature-of-things reasoning.
sbh1.3:63.37: Thus by these four reasonings the aggregate-teaching is examined.
sbh1.3:63.38: And whatever other teaching too — when, by these two modes (enumeration and examining-by-reasoning) it is rightly contemplated — that teaching's [contemplation] is called
sbh1.3:64.4: What follows will state the inward and outward obstacles;
sbh1.3:64.7: What, then, is the inward obstacle?
sbh1.3:64.8: When someone [Conjectural: has made no merit] in the past,
sbh1.3:64.9: and, [Conjectural: no merit having been done, does not obtain],
sbh1.3:64.10: from time to time, the requisites conforming to life,
sbh1.3:64.11: namely robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, and provisions; he has intense and prolonged lust,
sbh1.3:64.14: Or, again, he has previously committed actions that lead to illness,
sbh1.3:64.15: by which he is now full of illness —
sbh1.3:64.16: or in this very life he lives irregularly,
sbh1.3:64.17: whereby his wind, bile, or phlegm frequently rises, or indigestion settles in his body.
sbh1.3:64.19: of much business, much to do, frequently in large gatherings.
sbh1.3:64.20: Or fond of work, fond of speech, fond of sleep, fond of company, [Lacuna]
sbh1.3:64.21: or self-aggrandizing, fickle, heedless, dwelling in a bad place.
sbh1.3:64.22: Such are the inward obstacles, to be understood.
sbh1.3:64.24: As when he relies on bad persons,
sbh1.3:64.25: from whom he does not, from time to time, gain conforming advice and instruction;
sbh1.3:64.26: or when he dwells in a bad region —
sbh1.3:64.27: where, when he tries to settle in to dwell, by day there is a fierce, abundant sun-glare,
sbh1.3:64.29: loud noise, the clamor of a great crowd;
sbh1.3:64.30: or sharp contact of wind and sun, or danger even from humans — such are the outward obstacles, to be understood.
sbh1.3:64.31: Such, then, is the detailed division.
sbh1.3:65.3: the obstacle of application (*prayoga*), the obstacle of seclusion (*prāvivekya*),
sbh1.3:65.5: Of these, the obstacle of application: that obstacle which, when present and manifest, makes him incapable and unfit — completely, entirely — for any application to the wholesome side.
sbh1.3:65.7: When he becomes afflicted, gravely ill — his wind, bile, or phlegm is frequently disturbed, or indigestion (*viṣūcikā*) settles in his body;
sbh1.3:65.8: or when a scorpion bites him, or a centipede, or a human harasses him, or a non-human;
sbh1.3:65.9: or when he is not a gainer of robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, and provisions — such is the obstacle of application, to be understood.
sbh1.3:65.10: What is the obstacle of seclusion?
sbh1.3:65.11: When he becomes [over-]heavy in food, of much business, much to do, much to attend to; when he becomes fond of work and delights in it,
sbh1.3:65.12: his mind bent on those various duties;
sbh1.3:65.13: when he becomes fond of speech,
sbh1.3:65.15: for seclusion, exertion, retreat, and cultivation, he is content with mere recitation and study, fond of sleep,
sbh1.3:65.16: seized by sloth-and-torpor, of lazy disposition, cherishing the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of [lying on the] side, the pleasure of reclining;
sbh1.3:65.17: when he becomes fond of company with householders and renouncers,
sbh1.3:65.19: or thief-talk, food-talk, drink-talk, [Conjectural: clothes-talk], talk of courtesans, of streets, of the countryside, tales about great ministers, sea-stories —
sbh1.3:65.20: passing the time with such useless talk,
sbh1.3:65.21: delighting in it, much given to frequent gatherings of company,
sbh1.3:65.22: his mind scattered over those various matters,
sbh1.3:65.24: when he becomes fond of association,
sbh1.3:65.25: and pines for householders and renouncers who are absent;
sbh1.3:65.26: when he becomes fond of diversion (*prapañca*),
sbh1.3:65.27: delighting in diversion — in the forefront wherever there is something to go to, but in seclusion one who has laid down the burden —
sbh1.3:65.28: such are the dharmas to be understood as the obstacle of seclusion:
sbh1.3:65.29: [dharmas] by which, when present and manifest, it is not easy to dwell in remote lodgings in forests and woods,
sbh1.3:65.30: or at the foot of trees, or in empty huts.
sbh1.3:65.31: What is the obstacle of retreat?
sbh1.3:65.35: Of these, the obstacle of *śamatha*: [Conjectural: heedlessness] and dwelling in a bad place.
sbh1.3:65.36: When, in the heedless, sloth-and-torpor wraps the mind round,
sbh1.3:65.38: or inclines the mind toward slackness,
sbh1.3:65.39: or there is a darkened state of mind —
sbh1.3:65.40: and as for [obstacles arising] from dwelling in a bad place,
sbh1.3:65.41: there is a disturbance made by humans or from elsewhere,
sbh1.3:65.42: by which his mind is scattered outward. This is the obstacle of *śamatha*; it is to be understood as an obstacle of retreat. What is the obstacle of *vipaśyanā*?
sbh1.3:65.44: Of these, self-aggrandizement: when [he thinks] ‘I am of high family, gone forth,
sbh1.3:65.46: and others are not so,’ he exalts himself,
sbh1.3:65.49: Likewise [thinking], ‘I am gone forth from a wealthy family, not needy; I am handsome, well-favored, pleasing; I am much-learned, with a store [of learning];
sbh1.3:65.50: I am of fair speech, endowed with the faculty of speech — and other monks are not so’ —
sbh1.3:65.54: He, holding himself up [thus] — there are
sbh1.3:65.55: monks who are elders, [Conjectural: of long standing], deeply entered into the holy life — does not from time to time inquire of them,
sbh1.3:65.57: And they, in turn, do not from time to time open up to him the unopened points,
sbh1.3:65.58: [Conjectural: do not make plain the points not yet made plain],
sbh1.3:65.59: and do not reveal to him the deep meaning of the phrases,
sbh1.3:65.60: having penetrated it well and rightly by wisdom, even as far as the purification of knowledge-and-vision.
sbh1.3:65.64: Further, when he gains only a slight, scant, mere knowledge-and-vision, a mere dwelling at ease,
sbh1.3:65.66: that mere vision, he exalts himself,
sbh1.3:65.68: and being thus self-aggrandizing, is content with that much and does not strive further —
sbh1.3:65.69: thus too an obstacle is made for him
sbh1.3:65.70: through self-aggrandizement: namely, an obstacle to *vipaśyanā*.
sbh1.3:65.71: Or, again, fickle — of unpeaceful faculties,
sbh1.3:65.74: [Conjectural: speaking what is ill-spoken], doing what is ill-done — he does not firmly reflect on the dharmas,
sbh1.3:65.76: By this he does not bring *vipaśyanā* to fullness, does not purify it — thus fickleness too
sbh1.3:65.79: [In sum:] two dharmas are obstacles to *śamatha* —
sbh1.3:65.80: namely, heedlessness and dwelling in a bad place.
sbh1.3:65.81: Two dharmas are obstacles to *vipaśyanā* — namely, self-aggrandizement and fickleness.
sbh1.3:65.83: and whatever is the obstacle to *vipaśyanā* —
sbh1.3:65.84: this together is called the obstacle to retreat.
sbh1.3:65.85: And this is the summary meaning of obstacle.
sbh1.3:65.87: together with the previous detailed division —
sbh1.3:65.89: And by the reverse of this obstacle, *non-obstacle* is to be understood:
sbh1.3:65.90: the absence, departure, non-presence, and non-occurrence of these obstacles is what is called *non-obstacle*.
sbh1.3:66.2: That blameless gift which one gives for the sake of adorning the mind, for the sake of refining the mind, for the sake of the requisites of yoga, and for the attainment of the highest good.
sbh1.3:66.3: Here: who gives, to whom does one give, [Conjectural: what does one give], by what does one give,
sbh1.3:66.6: by which his giving becomes blameless.
sbh1.3:67.2: the giver and the patron give. [Lacuna]
sbh1.3:67.3: — this one is called the giver.
sbh1.3:67.4: The one whose own [thing] is given,
sbh1.3:67.5: and that by one who wants to give, not by one who does not — this one is called the patron (*dānapati*).
sbh1.3:67.6: And to whom does one give?
sbh1.3:67.8: one gives to four [kinds of recipient]:
sbh1.3:67.12: the pitiable, travelers, beggars, the blind, the deaf, the helpless, those without recourse, those lacking life-requisites —
sbh1.3:67.14: Helpers are: mother and father, wet-nurse, fosterer, rearer,
sbh1.3:67.15: or those who deliver one from a forest-wilderness, from famine, from fear of enemy armies, from bondage,
sbh1.3:67.16: or from sickness; and those who counsel one's welfare,
sbh1.3:67.17: counsel one's ease, bring about welfare and ease, help in matters that have arisen, share one's joys, share one's sorrows, and do not abandon one in danger — these and others of such kind are the helpers.
sbh1.3:67.21: love, respect, or devoted speech — those one talks with, knows well, holds dear —
sbh1.3:67.22: and others of such kind. These are called the dear.
sbh1.3:68.2: Recluses and brahmins reckoned as good —
sbh1.3:68.3: the non-harming, those who delight in non-harming; the lust-free and those practicing for the subduing of lust; the hatred-free and those practicing for the subduing of hatred;
sbh1.3:68.4: the delusion-free and those practicing for the subduing of delusion.
sbh1.3:68.5: These and others of such kind are called the distinguished.
sbh1.3:69.2: In brief, what is reckoned as sentient or reckoned as non-sentient —
sbh1.3:69.5: Namely the giving of son, female slave, male slave, worker, attendant, elephant, horse, cow, sheep, fowl, woman, man, boy, or girl —
sbh1.3:69.7: Or with respect to one's own body — hand, foot, head, flesh, blood, fat, and so on — he offers these.
sbh1.3:69.8: This [self-giving] too is a [Conjectural: sentient-reckoned] gift, [the kind] in which bodhisattvas are seen [to engage];
sbh1.3:69.9: but it is not the gift intended in the present context.
sbh1.3:69.10: [Here intended is rather:] all those [sentient beings] over whom he has lordship,
sbh1.3:69.12: and whom he is fit to bestow on others.
sbh1.3:69.13: Bestowing them, he makes himself blameless:
sbh1.3:69.14: others do not corrupt their minds on that account, for that reason;
sbh1.3:69.15: and the beings bestowed on others are [Conjectural: not] harmed by them — this is called the blameless gift of a sentient thing.
sbh1.3:70.4: Of these, wealth-things: gems, pearls, beryl, conch-shell, stone, coral, agate (*aśmagarbha*), *musāragalva*, gold, silver, red gems (*lohitikā*), [and] right-spiraling [shells];
sbh1.3:70.5: or any other such jewel, gold, silver, cloth, vessel or furniture, fragrance, or garland — this is called wealth.
sbh1.3:70.7: Whatever is food or drink: barley, rice, wheat, jujube, horse-gram, sesame, beans, sugar-cane juice, grape juice — or any other such thing. This is called grain.
sbh1.3:71.2: Namely: a field, a house, a shop, the establishment of a merit-hall or a monastery —
sbh1.3:71.3: or any other such thing. This is called land-thing.
sbh1.3:71.4: Of these, the sentient-reckoned thing [Lacuna] — this is what one gives.
sbh1.3:72.2: By volition accompanied by non-greed — that is, mind-formation, mental action —
sbh1.3:72.3: and by the bodily action produced therefrom,
sbh1.3:72.4: and the verbal action, for the relinquishing of the [Conjectural: thing to be given], in one's own continuum or [Lacuna] —
sbh1.3:72.8: with scriptural tradition as one's view, seeing the fruit, one gives respectfully;
sbh1.3:72.9: with humble mind, with one's own hand, with both hands;
sbh1.3:72.10: without contempt, at the right time;
sbh1.3:72.11: in such a way that the gift will be of use to others, without injuring [those others] in the giving;
sbh1.3:72.12: having acquired [it] by dharma, fairly, without violence, one gives what is clean,
sbh1.3:72.13: what is fine, what is allowable;
sbh1.3:72.14: [gives in such a way] that others are not made blameworthy [by accepting it],
sbh1.3:72.15: nor is oneself [made blameworthy by giving it];
sbh1.3:72.17: having disciplined the stain of stinginess and the stain of hoarding, one gives the gift;
sbh1.3:72.18: with glad mind before the giving, with mind clarified during the giving,
sbh1.3:72.19: and one is [Conjectural: not] remorseful afterward.
sbh1.3:72.24: namely, to the suffering; out of gratitude —
sbh1.3:72.25: namely, to the helpers; with love, respect, and devotion —
sbh1.3:72.26: namely, to the dear; with the prayer for worldly and otherworldly distinction —
sbh1.3:72.29: one gives’ — so it is said.
sbh1.3:72.30: By these modes — for him, whether householder or renouncer — for the sake of adorning the mind, for the sake of refining the mind,
sbh1.3:72.31: for the sake of the requisites of yoga, for the attainment of the highest good, that gift becomes blameless.
sbh1.3:73.1: What is the ornament of the recluse (*śramaṇālaṁkāra*)?
sbh1.3:73.2: When someone here is of faith,
sbh1.3:73.4: of little affliction, of aroused-energy nature, wise, of few desires, content,
sbh1.3:73.5: easily maintained, easily supported, endowed with ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*), pleasing, knowing measure,
sbh1.3:73.6: endowed with the dharmas of good persons,
sbh1.3:73.7: endowed with the dharmas of the wise,
sbh1.3:73.8: endowed with the marks of the wise,
sbh1.3:74.3: full of regard for the goal (*arthakalpanā*),
sbh1.3:74.4: [Conjectural: full of conviction], and willing in wholesome dharmas.
sbh1.3:74.5: He has clear faith in the Teacher,
sbh1.3:74.12: having honored, esteemed, respected, [and] worshiped, depending on him, he dwells [in practice].
sbh1.3:74.13: As toward the Teacher, so toward the Dharma,
sbh1.3:74.14: toward co-religionists, toward the training, toward advice and instruction, toward hospitality, toward heedfulness, toward concentration — thus he is of faith.
sbh1.3:74.16: He is [Conjectural: straight, of straight nature];
sbh1.3:74.17: he reveals himself as he actually is
sbh1.3:74.18: in the presence of the Teacher, the wise, [and his] co-religionists — thus he is non-deceitful.
sbh1.3:74.19: How is he of little affliction?
sbh1.3:74.21: he is endowed with a digestion that does its work in due time,
sbh1.3:74.22: not too hot, not too cold, unafflicted, naturally pleasant, by [the function of] which his eaten, drunk, chewed, [and] tasted [foods] are properly digested — thus he is of little affliction.
sbh1.3:74.23: How is he of aroused-energy nature?
sbh1.3:74.25: with energy, enthusiastic, of firm valor,
sbh1.3:74.26: one who has [Conjectural: not] laid down the burden in wholesome dharmas — skilled, not lazy, full of initiative;
sbh1.3:74.28: of bodily service for [his] wise co-religionists — thus he is of aroused energy.
sbh1.3:74.30: He is endowed with both mindfulness and intellect,
sbh1.3:74.31: of non-dull faculty, non-deluded faculty, not mute, capable of understanding the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken dharmas,
sbh1.3:74.35: How is he of few desires?
sbh1.3:74.36: Endowed with however many qualities — beginning with the state of few-desires — he does not seek to be known by others [for them]:
sbh1.3:74.37: [thinking] ‘would that others might know me as of few desires, or as endowed with such qualities’ — thus he is of few desires.
sbh1.3:74.39: With whatever robes, alms-food, [or] lodging, he is satisfied, content; [Conjectural: not having obtained] a robe, coarse or fine, he does not long for it,
sbh1.3:74.41: and having obtained, he uses [them] unattached,
sbh1.3:74.43: As with robes, so with alms-food [and] lodging. — How is he easily maintained?
sbh1.3:74.44: Only he himself is to be maintained by him,
sbh1.3:74.45: not others — such as servant-boys or [other] people,
sbh1.3:74.46: or any others on whose account he would undertake seeking,
sbh1.3:74.47: so that donors and patrons would think him ‘hard to maintain’.
sbh1.3:74.50: Even with little he gets along,
sbh1.3:74.51: even with inferior he gets along — thus he is easily supported.
sbh1.3:74.52: How is he endowed with ascetic qualities?
sbh1.3:74.55: a one-seat eater (*ekāsanika*), a later-food refuser (*khalupaścādbhaktika*),
sbh1.3:74.56: a three-robe wearer (*traicīvarika*), a felt-wearer (*nāmatika*), a refuse-rag wearer (*pāṁsukūlika*),
sbh1.3:74.57: a forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*), a tree-root dweller (*vṛkṣamūlika*), an open-air dweller (*ābhyavakāśika*),
sbh1.3:74.60: These [are] the twelve ascetic qualities, with reference to alms-food, robes, [and] lodging —
sbh1.3:74.62: [Counted as thirteen,] the alms-food-taker quality, when divided, becomes twofold:
sbh1.3:74.63: the [plain] alms-food-taker [who eats] as obtained, and the sequential alms-food-taker who, having begged from house to house, from family to family, and having completed the round, eats the alms-food as obtained, as suitable — and does not go up to houses with his nose in the air, [thinking]:
sbh1.3:74.64: ‘There I shall obtain fine chewable and edible food, enough to satisfy me.’
sbh1.3:74.65: When alms-food-taking is taken without distinction [as a single quality], they become twelve;
sbh1.3:74.66: when the [twofold] division is taken, thirteen.
sbh1.3:74.68: Seated in one [single] seat, however much should be eaten,
sbh1.3:74.70: once risen from that seat, he does not eat again.
sbh1.3:75.2: Seated for a meal, he does not [begin to] eat [it]
sbh1.3:75.3: until he has accepted all the food,
sbh1.3:75.4: [i.e.,] until he knows ‘I shall be able to maintain myself [with this much]’;
sbh1.3:75.5: when he knows ‘beyond this no further food shall be needful for me,’
sbh1.3:75.6: then, having put aside everything [else, refusing more], he begins
sbh1.3:75.8: Thus he is a later-food refuser.
sbh1.3:75.9: How is he a three-robe wearer?
sbh1.3:75.10: With [just] three robes he gets along — saṅghāṭi, upper robe, [and] inner robe;
sbh1.3:75.11: he does not keep more than three robes — thus he is a three-robe wearer.
sbh1.3:77.2: three robes or extra robes — all that he wears is woolen,
sbh1.3:77.5: How is he a refuse-rag wearer (*pāṁsukūlika*)?
sbh1.3:77.6: Whatever robe has been left by others,
sbh1.3:77.7: discarded — on the road, in the lane, at the crossroads, at a junction, on the path or off-path; mixed with feces, mixed with urine, [or] mingled with feces, urine, pus, blood, [or] spittle —
sbh1.3:77.8: from which he removes what is impure, [and,] taking the [usable] substance, cleansing [it], sewing [it], dyeing [it], wears [it] — thus he is a refuse-rag wearer.
sbh1.3:77.10: He dwells in remote forest-thicket lodgings,
sbh1.3:77.11: those distant from villages and market-towns — thus he is a forest-dweller.
sbh1.3:78.1: How is he a tree-root dweller (*vṛkṣamūlika*)?
sbh1.3:78.2: He makes his abode at the foot of a tree,
sbh1.3:78.4: Thus he is a tree-root dweller.
sbh1.3:78.5: How is he an open-air dweller (*ābhyavakāśika*)?
sbh1.3:78.6: He makes his abode in the open air,
sbh1.3:78.8: Thus he is an open-air dweller.
sbh1.3:78.9: How is he a cemetery dweller (*śmāśānika*)?
sbh1.3:78.10: He makes his abode in a cemetery, [the place] where the dead are
sbh1.3:78.11: carried out — thus he is a cemetery dweller.
sbh1.3:79.2: On couch, stool, [or] grass-mat, he passes the time [only] by sitting,
sbh1.3:79.3: not leaning his back or side against a couch, stool, wall, tree-root, grass-mat, or leaf-mat — thus he is a sitter.
sbh1.3:79.4: How is he an any-bed acceptor (*yāthāsaṁstarika*)?
sbh1.3:79.5: Wherever — on grass-mat or leaf-mat — he prepares the bed:
sbh1.3:79.6: whatever grass-mat or leaf-mat has been once arranged,
sbh1.3:79.7: just so he uses [it as] the bed,
sbh1.3:79.8: he does not disturb it again,
sbh1.3:79.9: nor re-arrange it — thus he is an any-bed acceptor.
sbh1.3:79.10: Why are these called ‘ascetic qualities’ (*dhutaguṇa*)? Namely, just as wool or cotton, when shaken (*dhuta*), becomes loose,
sbh1.3:79.11: and at that time is soft,
sbh1.3:79.12: light, [and] workable — namely for making thread or [Conjectural: felt bedding] —
sbh1.3:79.13: just so, for someone here, by lust for alms-food the mind is attached to alms-food,
sbh1.3:79.14: joined together [with it]; by lust for robes [Lacuna]; by lust for lodging the mind is attached to lodging,
sbh1.3:79.16: He, by these ascetic qualities, purifies [it], straightens [it],
sbh1.3:79.17: makes [it] soft, workable, straight, compliant, tractable — namely for dwelling in the holy life; therefore they are called ‘ascetic qualities.’
sbh1.3:80.1: Now, for the abandonment of lust for fine food in alms-food, he becomes a one-seat eater.
sbh1.3:80.2: For the abandonment of lust for plentiful food, he becomes a felt-wearer.
sbh1.3:80.3: For the abandonment of lust for fine robes, he becomes a felt-wearer.
sbh1.3:80.4: For the abandonment of lust for fine robes, he becomes a three-robe wearer.
sbh1.3:80.5: For the abandonment of lust for soft-contact robes, he becomes a refuse-rag wearer.
sbh1.3:80.9: lust for side-comfort and lying-down comfort,
sbh1.3:80.11: Now, for the abandonment of association-lust, he becomes a forest-dweller.
sbh1.3:80.12: For the abandonment of shelter-lust, he becomes a tree-root dweller [or] an open-air dweller,
sbh1.3:80.14: Moreover, cemetery-dwelling is also for the abandonment of [Conjectural: sexual lust].
sbh1.3:80.15: For the abandonment of lust for side-comfort and lying-down comfort, he becomes a sitter.
sbh1.3:80.16: For the abandonment of lust for spread, coverlet, [and] covering, he becomes an any-bed acceptor. — Thus he is endowed with ascetic qualities.
sbh1.3:80.18: He is endowed with pleasing setting-forth-and-returning, looking ahead, looking around, bending and stretching, [and] wearing of saṅghāṭi, robes, [and] bowl — thus he is pleasing.
sbh1.3:80.19: How is he knowing the right measure?
sbh1.3:80.20: When faithful brāhmaṇas and householders [Conjectural: press him to take freely] —
sbh1.3:80.21: namely robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites for illness — in accepting them, he knows the measure.
sbh1.3:80.22: Thus he is knowing the right measure.
sbh1.3:80.23: How is he endowed with the dharmas of good persons?
sbh1.3:80.24: Gone forth from a high family, or from a wealthy family, handsome, well-favored to see, pleasing, much-learned, [Conjectural: endowed with the speech-faculty],
sbh1.3:80.25: [or being] a gainer of some kind of mere knowledge, mere vision, [or] mere dwelling at ease — by these he [Conjectural: does not] exalt himself,
sbh1.3:80.27: he practices Dharma in accordance with Dharma — thus he is endowed with the dharmas of good persons. — How is he endowed with the marks of the wise?
sbh1.3:80.28: The fool is action-marked, [and] the wise [too] is action-marked.
sbh1.3:80.29: How [so]? The fool is an ill-thought-out thinker,
sbh1.3:80.30: an ill-spoken speaker, an ill-done-doer. The wise, on the other hand, is a well-thought-out thinker,
sbh1.3:80.32: Thus he is endowed with the marks of the wise.
sbh1.3:80.34: Abused, he does not abuse in return;
sbh1.3:80.35: angered [against], he does not anger in return;
sbh1.3:80.36: [Conjectural: struck, he does not strike back];
sbh1.3:80.37: reviled, he does not revile in return.
sbh1.3:80.38: And that venerable one is patient —
sbh1.3:80.39: of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, of contact with gnats, mosquitoes, wind, sun, [and] creeping things; of ill-spoken, ill-come ways of speech from others;
sbh1.3:80.40: of bodily feelings — painful, intense, harsh, biting, disagreeable, life-threatening — he is patient, of accommodating nature.
sbh1.3:80.43: When [he is] endowed with friendly bodily action,
sbh1.3:80.44: with friendly verbal action and friendly mental action in the presence of the Teacher; and with wise co-religionists he is a sharer in common [Damaged],
sbh1.3:80.45: not one who eats in secret,
sbh1.3:80.46: of gains lawful and Dharma-obtained, what is in the bowl, what the bowl holds; and he is sharing in virtue
sbh1.3:80.48: He, endowed with these six conciliatory dharmas — making one dear, making one respected, [Conjectural: making for non-dispute] — becomes pleasant to live with,
sbh1.3:80.55: Free from frowning, of open-faced complexion, accompanied by a smile, the first to greet,
sbh1.3:80.60: He, endowed with these dharmas, is desirous of Dharma,
sbh1.3:80.62: not desirous of gain, honor, fame, [or] eulogy.
sbh1.3:80.63: He is not endowed with the wrong view of superimposing [what does not exist],
sbh1.3:80.64: nor with [the wrong view] of depreciating [what does exist];
sbh1.3:80.65: he does not superimpose a dharma that does not exist,
sbh1.3:80.66: nor depreciate a dharma that does.
sbh1.3:80.68: of spoken [word] or [Conjectural: poetry] — letters, words, and phrases that are [mere] signs, connected with Lokāyata —
sbh1.3:80.70: and knowing this, he avoids it from afar;
sbh1.3:80.71: he does not delight in it, does not take pleasure in it; and [Conjectural: he does not keep extra] robes.
sbh1.3:80.78: [thinking:] ‘lest on their account there be for me, in many ways, distraction or busyness; or, when they change and become otherwise, there arise sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and distress.’
sbh1.3:80.79: And the defilements and secondary defilements as they arise he does not accommodate,
sbh1.3:80.80: [but] abandons, dispels, [and] puts an end to [them],
sbh1.3:80.81: [thinking:] ‘lest from that, on that account, there arise either present-life suffering or future-life suffering.’
sbh1.3:80.82: And he does not let [Conjectural: what is given in faith] go to waste.
sbh1.3:80.84: of unfallen vow, he uses what is given in faith,
sbh1.3:80.85: and he does not reject what is given in faith;
sbh1.3:80.87: He is a seeker of his own faults and slip-ups,
sbh1.3:80.88: a concealer of [his own] good, a revealer of [his own] evil.
sbh1.3:80.89: In others’ faults and slip-ups he does not engage; he does not [Conjectural: deliberately] fall into an offence,
sbh1.3:80.90: even for the sake of [his] life;
sbh1.3:80.91: and if he has fallen [into one], he quickly, very quickly makes amends according to Dharma.
sbh1.3:80.92: In duties to be done he is skilled, non-lazy, a self-doer, not seeking bodily service from others.
sbh1.3:80.93: And he has confident conviction in the inconceivable greatness of the Buddhas and Buddha-disciples, and in the deep teaching,
sbh1.3:80.95: ‘Only the Tathāgatas are the knowers and seers [of this]; not I.’
sbh1.3:80.96: Having seen thus, he does not himself become one who stands on clinging to [his own] view, who grasps what is improper, [Conjectural: who is hard to make let go].
sbh1.3:80.97: He, endowed with these qualities, so dwelling, so training, adorned with the ornament of the recluse, shines — just as some young man, [Conjectural: fond of adornment], an enjoyer of sense-pleasures, bathed and anointed,
sbh1.3:80.100: namely with necklaces, armlets, ring on the finger, or garland of gold and silver —
sbh1.3:80.101: just so he, adorned with the various recluse-ornament qualities,
sbh1.3:80.103: Therefore it is called ornament of the recluse.
sbh1.3:80.104: This is called the ornament of the recluse.
sbh1.3:82.2: food, wakefulness, dwelling with full awareness,
sbh1.3:83.1: [Lacuna] and likewise hearing-and-reflection on the true dharma,
sbh1.3:83.2: non-obstacle, generosity, and the ornament [of the recluse] last.
sbh1.3:84.1: Faith, non-deceit, little affliction, energy, wisdom, few desires, contentment, ease of being cared for,
sbh1.3:85.1: ease of support, the ascetic qualities, pleasingness, knowing-measure, [Lacuna] patience, gentleness, amiability.
sbh1.3:86.1: In the Yogācārabhūmi, comprised in the Śrāvakabhūmi, the first yogasthāna [is complete].
